questions.title: NOT IN vs. NOT EXISTS with NULLs
questions.prompt: A colleague writes a query using `WHERE CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT CustomerID FROM Returns)` to find customers who never returned anything, and it comes back with zero rows even though you know some customers have never returned a product. What's going wrong, and how would you rewrite it?
questions.modelAnswer: NOT IN is built on a chain of OR-ed inequality comparisons under the hood, and any comparison against NULL in SQL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. If even a single row in the Returns.CustomerID subquery is NULL, the whole NOT IN expression collapses to UNKNOWN for every outer row, because 'not equal to NULL' can never be proven true, and SQL's three-valued logic means the entire OR chain can't be guaranteed TRUE either. The result is zero rows, even though the intent was obviously satisfiable. NOT EXISTS avoids the problem entirely because it uses a correlated existence check rather than a value comparison -- it asks 'does at least one matching row exist,' and a NULL in the subquery's column never participates in that logic, since EXISTS never actually compares values. The fix is almost always to replace NOT IN with NOT EXISTS plus a correlated subquery, or to add a WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL filter inside the IN subquery if NOT IN must be kept for some reason.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those T-SQL gotchas I actually check for by habit now, because it's bitten me before. The first thing I'd do is run SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Returns WHERE CustomerID IS NULL -- if that comes back non-zero, I've found the bug immediately, because NOT IN's logic breaks down the moment the subquery can return even one NULL. Rather than patching it with an IS NOT NULL filter inside the subquery, which works but is easy to forget to apply the next time the query gets copied somewhere else, I'd just rewrite the whole thing as NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery. It sidesteps the NULL problem structurally instead of relying on someone remembering to filter NULLs out, and in my experience it also tends to get a better execution plan from the optimizer on larger tables.
commonMistakes: Not realizing a single NULL in the NOT IN subquery's column silently zeroes out the entire result
Patching the symptom with IS NOT NULL inside the subquery instead of switching to the structurally safer NOT EXISTS
Assuming NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are always interchangeable, rather than understanding they handle NULLs differently
Debugging the outer query's logic first instead of checking the subquery's column for NULLs, which is almost always the real cause
keyPoints: NOT IN compares against each subquery value; any NULL among them makes the whole expression UNKNOWN
SQL's three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) is the root cause, not a bug in NOT IN itself
NOT EXISTS uses correlated existence checks, which are immune to NULLs in the subquery column
The safe fix is rewriting as NOT EXISTS, not just filtering NULLs out of the IN subquery as a patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the NULL-driven root cause
Explains three-valued logic (UNKNOWN) accurately
Provides a correct NOT EXISTS rewrite

questions.title: READ COMMITTED vs. snapshot isolation
questions.prompt: What does the default READ COMMITTED isolation level actually protect against in SQL Server, what can still go wrong under it, and how does enabling RCSI (read committed snapshot isolation) change the picture?
questions.modelAnswer: READ COMMITTED guarantees a reader never sees uncommitted ('dirty') data from another transaction that's still in flight -- it only reads data that has already been committed. Under the default, pessimistic version of READ COMMITTED, that guarantee is enforced with locks: a reader takes a shared lock, and if a row is currently being modified by another transaction holding an exclusive lock, the reader blocks until that writer commits or rolls back. This prevents dirty reads, but it does not prevent non-repeatable reads -- if a transaction reads the same row twice, a concurrent committed update in between can make the second read return a different value -- and it means readers and writers can block each other, which is a common source of contention on busy OLTP tables. RCSI changes the mechanism without changing the isolation level's name: instead of blocking on a writer's lock, a reader under RCSI is handed the last-committed version of the row from a row-versioning store in tempdb, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The tradeoff is overhead in tempdb for storing those row versions, and the read is a point-in-time snapshot as of the start of the statement, not a live view of a currently-in-progress write.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as 'same isolation guarantee, different enforcement mechanism.' Plain READ COMMITTED still guarantees I never read a half-written row from someone else's uncommitted transaction, but it enforces that with locking, so if I'm reading a row someone else is actively updating, I just wait. That's the blocking people complain about on a busy table during business hours. RCSI keeps the exact same 'no dirty reads' promise but swaps locking for row versioning in tempdb -- when I read a row that's being modified, I get served the last committed version instead of waiting, so my read and their write don't block each other at all. I'd flag the real tradeoff honestly in an interview: RCSI isn't free, it adds load to tempdb, and because my read reflects a snapshot as of when my statement started, I need to be comfortable that I'm not seeing an update that committed a split second after my query began.
commonMistakes: Assuming READ COMMITTED prevents non-repeatable reads, when it only prevents dirty reads
Thinking RCSI is a separate isolation level with different read guarantees, rather than READ COMMITTED enforced via versioning instead of locking
Not mentioning the tempdb overhead RCSI introduces as a real operational cost
Believing RCSI eliminates all blocking in the database, rather than specifically reader/writer blocking on READ COMMITTED reads
keyPoints: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, not non-repeatable reads
Default READ COMMITTED enforces this with shared/exclusive locks, causing reader/writer blocking
RCSI enforces the same guarantee via tempdb row versioning instead of locks
RCSI removes reader/writer blocking at the cost of tempdb overhead and snapshot semantics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what READ COMMITTED does and doesn't prevent
Correctly explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism
States the practical tradeoff (tempdb overhead, snapshot semantics)

questions.title: What actually happens during a deadlock
questions.prompt: Walk through what a deadlock actually is in SQL Server, why error 1205 specifically names a 'deadlock victim,' and what that tells the application that receives it.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other one needs, and each is waiting for the other to release it -- a classic example is Transaction A holding a lock on Row 1 and waiting to lock Row 2, while Transaction B holds a lock on Row 2 and is waiting to lock Row 1. Neither can proceed and neither will ever release its lock voluntarily, so without intervention both would wait forever. SQL Server runs a background deadlock monitor that periodically checks for exactly this cycle, and when it finds one, it picks one of the two transactions as the 'deadlock victim' -- usually the one that would be cheapest to roll back, based on the estimated cost of undoing its work -- and kills it, rolling back all of its changes and raising error 1205 to whoever issued it. The other transaction is left to proceed normally. The key thing error 1205 communicates to the calling application is that the transaction didn't fail because of bad data or logic -- it was deliberately sacrificed to break a deadlock -- so the correct response is almost always to retry the whole transaction from the start, not to treat it as a permanent failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as two transactions stuck in a standoff: A is holding what B wants, B is holding what A wants, and neither will budge, so left alone they'd both wait forever. SQL Server doesn't let that happen indefinitely -- a deadlock monitor thread wakes up on an interval, detects the cycle, and picks one of the two transactions to kill off as the 'victim,' generally the cheaper one to roll back. That transaction gets error 1205 and its work is fully undone; the other one just continues like nothing happened. The important part for how I'd build around this is that 1205 isn't really an error in the normal sense -- it's SQL Server's way of saying 'this had to be sacrificed, try again.' So any application code that's going to run transactions against a busy table needs retry logic specifically watching for 1205, because treating it as a fatal error instead of a transient, retryable one will cause work to get dropped that should have just succeeded on a second attempt.
commonMistakes: Describing a deadlock as 'the database being slow' rather than two transactions each blocked on a lock the other holds
Not knowing SQL Server actively detects and resolves deadlocks rather than letting them hang forever
Treating error 1205 as a permanent failure instead of a transient one that calls for a retry
Assuming the victim is chosen randomly rather than based on estimated rollback cost
keyPoints: A deadlock is a circular wait: each transaction holds a lock the other needs
SQL Server's deadlock monitor detects the cycle and kills one transaction as the victim
The victim is typically chosen by lowest estimated rollback cost
Error 1205 signals a transient, retryable failure -- application code should retry the transaction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the circular-wait mechanism of a deadlock
Explains how the deadlock monitor resolves it and picks a victim
Correctly states the application-level implication (retry logic)

questions.title: Clustered vs. nonclustered indexes
questions.prompt: What's the structural difference between a clustered index and a nonclustered index, why can a table have only one clustered index but many nonclustered ones, and what's a 'key lookup' in an execution plan?
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order the table's rows are stored in on disk -- the table's data pages themselves are sorted by the clustered index key, which is why a table can have at most one: the rows can only physically exist in one order at a time. A nonclustered index is a separate structure entirely: it's its own sorted copy of just the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the corresponding row in the clustered index (or, if there's no clustered index, a direct row locator). Because a nonclustered index is a distinct, self-contained object, a table can have many of them, each organized around different columns for different query patterns. A 'key lookup' shows up in an execution plan when a query filters using a nonclustered index -- which quickly finds the matching rows' pointers -- but also needs columns that aren't stored in that nonclustered index itself, forcing SQL Server to follow each pointer back to the clustered index to fetch the rest of the row. On a query returning many rows, that's one extra random-access read per row, which is often the single biggest cost in the plan and the reason query tuning frequently focuses on adding 'included columns' to a nonclustered index to eliminate the lookup entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the clustered index as the table, not as something separate sitting on top of it -- whatever column you cluster on is literally the physical sort order the data lives in, which is exactly why you only get one. A nonclustered index is more like an index card system off to the side: it's sorted by whatever columns you put in it, and each card points back to where the real row lives. You can have as many of those card systems as make sense for your query patterns. The key lookup is the cost I watch for most in an execution plan -- it means the nonclustered index got me to the right rows fast, but then had to go fetch extra columns from the clustered index one row at a time to finish the job. If I see a thick arrow feeding into a key lookup on a query that runs constantly, my first instinct is to check whether adding the missing columns as INCLUDE columns on the nonclustered index would let it satisfy the whole query without that extra trip.
questions.example:
-- Nonclustered index covering filter column but not SELECT columns forces a key lookup
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID
    ON dbo.Orders (CustomerID);

-- Adding INCLUDE columns can eliminate the key lookup for this specific query
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID_Covering
    ON dbo.Orders (CustomerID)
    INCLUDE (OrderDate, TotalAmount);
commonMistakes: Thinking a table can have multiple clustered indexes, rather than exactly zero or one
Not understanding that a nonclustered index stores pointers back to the clustered index, not full rows
Missing key lookups as a performance red flag in an execution plan
Assuming adding more nonclustered indexes is always free, ignoring the write/storage overhead of maintaining each one
keyPoints: A clustered index defines the physical storage order of the table -- only one per table
A nonclustered index is a separate, sorted structure with pointers back to the real row
A table can have many nonclustered indexes for different query patterns
A key lookup is the extra trip back to the clustered index when a nonclustered index doesn't cover all needed columns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered index's physical-ordering role
Correctly explains nonclustered index structure and pointers
Correctly defines a key lookup and its performance implication

questions.title: SCD Type 2 in plain terms
questions.prompt: What problem does a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 solve that simply overwriting a dimension row (Type 1) doesn't, and what columns does a Type 2 implementation typically need to add?
questions.modelAnswer: A Type 1 update to a dimension simply overwrites the old attribute value with the new one in place -- if a customer's address changes, the old address is gone, and every fact row that was ever associated with that customer now implicitly reports the new address, even for historical transactions that actually happened at the old address. That's fine when history genuinely doesn't matter, but it silently falsifies historical reporting whenever it does. A Type 2 change instead preserves history by never overwriting the old row: when an attribute changes, the existing row is marked as no longer current (typically via an EndDate and an IsCurrent flag), and a brand new row is inserted with a new surrogate key, the updated attribute value, a StartDate, and IsCurrent set to true. Fact tables that were loaded before the change continue to point at the old surrogate key, so a sales report run today still correctly shows that a sale happened while the customer lived at their old address, while new fact rows loaded going forward point at the new surrogate key. The typical added columns are a surrogate key (separate from the natural/business key, since now there can be multiple rows per business key), EffectiveStartDate, EffectiveEndDate (or NULL for the current row), and an IsCurrent boolean flag for easy filtering to 'the dimension as it looks right now.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with why anyone bothers with this complexity instead of just overwriting the row. If a customer moves and I use Type 1, I've just rewritten history -- every past sale now reports their new address, even sales that happened while they lived somewhere else. Type 2 is how a dimension preserves that history honestly: instead of updating the row, I close it out with an end date, flip IsCurrent to false, and insert a brand new row with a new surrogate key for the updated attribute. The fact table doesn't change at all -- old fact rows still point at the old surrogate key, so old reports stay accurate, and new fact rows loaded from today onward naturally pick up the new surrogate key. The piece that trips people up building their first Type 2 dimension is remembering the surrogate key has to be separate from the natural key, because with Type 2 there's no longer a one-to-one relationship between a business entity and a dimension row -- there can be several rows for the same customer over time.
commonMistakes: Confusing Type 1 (overwrite) and Type 2 (preserve history with a new row) behaviors
Forgetting that a Type 2 dimension needs a surrogate key distinct from the natural/business key
Not realizing fact rows loaded before a change correctly keep pointing at the old surrogate key, which is what preserves historical accuracy
Omitting IsCurrent or an end-date column, making it hard to efficiently query 'the dimension as it is right now'
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrites in place and loses history; Type 2 preserves it
Type 2 closes the old row and inserts a new row with a new surrogate key on change
Fact rows loaded before the change keep referencing the old surrogate key, preserving historical accuracy
Typical added columns: surrogate key, EffectiveStartDate, EffectiveEndDate, IsCurrent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the history-preservation problem Type 2 solves
Correctly describes the row-versioning mechanism (close old, insert new)
Names the typical added columns correctly

questions.title: dbt's four materializations
questions.prompt: dbt gives you a choice of view, table, incremental, or ephemeral materialization for a model. What does each one actually do under the hood, and what's a sensible default for a staging model versus a large fact-table model?
questions.modelAnswer: view materializes a model as a database VIEW -- the SQL runs fresh against the underlying tables every time something queries it, so it's always current but pays the full query cost on every read. table materializes it as an actual physical TABLE: dbt runs a CREATE TABLE AS (or equivalent) on every dbt run, fully rebuilding the table from scratch, which is fast to query afterward but potentially expensive to rebuild if the model scans a lot of source data. incremental is built for large, append-or-update-heavy models: instead of rebuilding the whole table every run, dbt only processes new or changed rows since the last run (using a configured incremental strategy like append or merge) and folds them into the existing table, which is dramatically cheaper for a table with history that doesn't need to be reprocessed from scratch every time. ephemeral doesn't create any database object at all -- it's inlined as a CTE directly into whatever model references it at compile time, which is useful for small, reusable intermediate logic that doesn't need its own object but adds compile-time complexity if overused. A lightweight staging model that just does light cleanup over a source table is a reasonable view (cheap to maintain, always fresh) or table if it's queried heavily downstream; a large fact table with years of history is the textbook case for incremental, since fully rebuilding it from scratch on every run would be wasteful and slow.
questions.professionalAnswer: I pick the materialization based on how expensive the model is to rebuild versus how often it's queried. A thin staging model that's mostly renaming and light casting over a source table, I'd default to view -- it's basically free to maintain and always reflects the latest data, and if it turns out to be queried heavily I can bump it to table later with a one-line config change. A big fact table with years of transaction history is a different story -- rebuilding that from scratch as a table on every single dbt run would mean reprocessing years of unchanged data every night, so that's exactly when I reach for incremental, configuring it to only pick up new or changed rows since the last run. I use ephemeral sparingly, mostly for a small, single-purpose CTE-like model that a couple of other models share but that doesn't deserve its own table or view in the warehouse -- overusing it just makes the compiled SQL harder to debug since the logic gets inlined invisibly.
commonMistakes: Defaulting every model to table materialization regardless of size or query frequency, wasting compute on unnecessary full rebuilds
Using incremental on a small model where a full table rebuild would already be cheap and simple
Not realizing ephemeral models create no database object and are inlined as CTEs at compile time
Forgetting that a view always runs the underlying SQL fresh, meaning its query cost is paid on every single read, not once at build time
keyPoints: view: runs the SQL fresh on every query, no stored data
table: fully rebuilt as a physical table on every run
incremental: only processes new/changed rows since the last run
ephemeral: no database object, inlined as a CTE at compile time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains all four materializations
Gives a sensible default choice for staging vs. large fact models
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Airflow trigger rules
questions.prompt: By default, an Airflow task only runs if every one of its upstream dependencies succeeded. What is that default trigger rule called, and what do the one_success and none_failed trigger rules each change about that behavior?
questions.modelAnswer: The default trigger rule is all_success: a task only becomes eligible to run once every one of its direct upstream tasks has finished with a success status; if even one upstream task fails or is skipped, the downstream task is skipped too (and that skip propagates further downstream unless something changes the rule again). one_success changes that to an OR condition: the downstream task runs as soon as at least one of its upstream tasks succeeds, regardless of whether the others failed or are still skipped -- a common use is a branching pattern where only one of several parallel branches is expected to actually run, and a task after the branch point still needs to execute once any branch completes. none_failed is more permissive than all_success but stricter than one_success: it runs the downstream task as long as no upstream task has an explicit failed status, allowing upstream tasks that were skipped (not failed) to not block it -- this is the standard trigger rule for a cleanup or notification task that should run whether the main work succeeded or was intentionally skipped, but not if something actually failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about trigger rules in terms of what failure mode I'm trying to tolerate downstream. all_success, the default, is the strict case -- every single upstream task has to have actually succeeded, and if anything failed or got skipped, my task gets skipped too, and that skip keeps cascading. one_success is what I reach for after a branching task, where only one branch is actually going to run and the rest get skipped on purpose -- the task that reconverges after the branch needs one_success so it doesn't wait on branches that were never going to execute. none_failed is the one I use most for cleanup-style tasks, like a notification or a temp-table drop that I want to run regardless of whether upstream work succeeded, as long as nothing actually failed outright -- it tolerates skipped upstream tasks, which all_success wouldn't, but still won't fire if something genuinely broke.
commonMistakes: Assuming all_success tolerates skipped upstream tasks, when a skip blocks it just like a failure does
Using one_success for a cleanup task that should run after a genuine failure too, when none_failed is usually the better fit
Not knowing a skip propagates downstream by default, silently skipping an entire branch of the DAG
Confusing trigger rules with retries -- trigger rules decide whether a task runs at all based on upstream state, not how many times a single task retries
keyPoints: all_success (default): every upstream task must have succeeded
one_success: runs as soon as at least one upstream task succeeds
none_failed: runs as long as no upstream task explicitly failed, tolerating skips
Skips propagate downstream by default unless a different trigger rule changes that

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the default all_success behavior
Correctly explains one_success
Correctly explains none_failed and how it differs from one_success

questions.title: Kafka delivery semantics, precisely
questions.prompt: Kafka is often described as supporting 'exactly-once' delivery, but that phrase hides a lot of nuance. What do at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once actually mean in terms of producer and consumer behavior, and what specific settings move you between them?
questions.modelAnswer: At-most-once means a record might be delivered zero or one times, but never more than once -- if a producer sends a record and doesn't wait for or retry on acknowledgment failure, a dropped message is simply lost, which is the cheapest but least safe option. At-least-once means a record is delivered one or more times -- never lost, but a retry after an ambiguous failure (the broker actually wrote it, but the acknowledgment back to the producer was lost) can cause the same record to be written twice, so downstream consumers must handle duplicates. This is the practical default most teams run with: producers set acks=all so a write is only considered successful once it's been replicated to every in-sync replica, and retries are enabled so transient failures are retried rather than silently dropped -- but a retried-after-ambiguous-failure write is still a real risk, hence 'at least' once. Exactly-once is achieved specifically by enabling idempotent producers (enable.idempotence=true, which Kafka uses to assign a sequence number per producer session so the broker can detect and drop a duplicate retry), combined with transactional writes when a consume-process-produce pipeline needs the read, the processing, and the write to all commit together atomically. On the consumer side, exactly-once processing also requires disabling naive auto-commit of offsets (or being very deliberate about when offsets commit relative to when output is actually written) so a crash between processing and offset commit doesn't either skip or reprocess a record.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this from least to most guaranteed, because that's genuinely how the mental model builds. At-most-once is 'fire and forget' -- if the ack never comes back, I just move on, so a dropped record on the wire is gone forever; nobody actually wants this for anything that matters. At-least-once is the realistic default -- acks=all plus retries means I never lose a record, but a retry after a broker actually wrote the message but the ack got lost on the way back to me means I might send it again, so now my consumer has to be fine seeing the same record twice. Getting to true exactly-once takes a specific combination: enable.idempotence=true on the producer, so Kafka tags each write with a sequence number and the broker silently drops an exact duplicate retry instead of writing it twice, plus transactions if I'm reading from one topic and writing to another and need that whole read-process-write cycle to be atomic. And I always point out that exactly-once semantics are about the Kafka pipeline itself -- if my consumer's actual side effect is, say, calling an external API that isn't itself idempotent, Kafka's guarantees don't extend past the Kafka boundary.
commonMistakes: Treating 'exactly-once' as a single on/off switch rather than a specific combination of idempotent producers and transactional writes
Assuming acks=all alone gives exactly-once delivery, when it's actually what at-least-once relies on
Forgetting that naive auto-commit of consumer offsets can cause message loss or reprocessing independent of producer settings
Not recognizing that Kafka's exactly-once guarantee only covers the Kafka pipeline itself, not a non-idempotent external side effect downstream
keyPoints: At-most-once: records can be lost, never duplicated
At-least-once: records are never lost but can be duplicated on retry; the common production default
Exactly-once requires enable.idempotence=true plus transactions for read-process-write pipelines
Consumer offset-commit timing also affects whether records are skipped or reprocessed on failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three delivery semantics
Correctly identifies the specific settings (acks=all, enable.idempotence, transactions)
Notes the consumer-side offset-commit nuance

deepDive.heading: Why idempotent producers don't need application-level dedup
deepDive.content: When enable.idempotence=true is set, Kafka assigns each producer a unique Producer ID (PID) and tags every message with a per-partition sequence number. The broker keeps track of the last sequence number it committed for each PID/partition pair, so if a retry arrives with a sequence number it's already seen, it silently acknowledges success without writing the record again. This closes the specific gap that causes duplicates under plain at-least-once: a retry after a lost acknowledgment (not a lost write) can no longer create a second copy, because the broker itself recognizes and discards the exact duplicate. It's important to be precise about scope, though -- idempotence protects against producer retries specifically; it does not deduplicate two genuinely separate send() calls with the same business-level payload, and it does not extend any guarantee to consumers or to whatever the consumer does with the message downstream.

deepDive.heading: Where transactions come in for consume-process-produce
deepDive.content: A common principal-level follow-up is: what if my pipeline reads from topic A, transforms the record, and writes to topic B? Idempotent producers alone don't make that whole cycle atomic. Kafka transactions solve this by letting a producer group a batch of writes to one or more topics together with the offset commit for the records it consumed, so either the entire unit -- the new output records and the updated consumer offset -- commits together, or none of it does. That's what lets a stream-processing job claim true exactly-once semantics end to end within Kafka, rather than just exactly-once production to a single topic.

questions.title: How Snowflake warehouses are billed
questions.prompt: How is compute actually billed in Snowflake, what does auto-suspend do, and why does scaling out with a multi-cluster warehouse not create the same contention that scaling up a single warehouse would?
questions.modelAnswer: A Snowflake virtual warehouse is billed per-second (with a typical 60-second minimum per resume) for however long it's actually running, based on its size (X-Small through 6X-Large and beyond), regardless of how much or how little work it's actually doing while running -- an idle warehouse that's still 'up' still costs money. auto-suspend addresses exactly that: after a configured period of no queries, Snowflake automatically suspends the warehouse, stopping the billing clock, and auto-resume brings it back online transparently the moment a new query arrives, at the cost of a brief resume latency. Scaling a single warehouse 'up' (say, from Small to Large) gives that one cluster more compute per query, which helps an individual slow query but does nothing for a flood of many concurrent small queries all competing for the same cluster's queue. A multi-cluster warehouse instead scales 'out': Snowflake automatically spins up additional clusters of the same size when queueing is detected, so simultaneous queries get routed across multiple independent clusters rather than piling up behind each other on one, and scales back down once demand drops -- this is specifically a concurrency solution, not a per-query speed solution, which is the distinction interviewers are usually probing for.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always separate these into two different cost/performance levers because people conflate them. Warehouse size is about how much horsepower a single query gets -- if one query is slow because it's scanning a lot of data, bumping the warehouse size can genuinely speed that one query up. Multi-cluster is a completely different lever -- it's about what happens when fifty people run dashboards at 9am and they'd otherwise all queue up behind one warehouse; Snowflake just spins up more clusters of the same size to absorb the concurrent load, then spins them back down. On cost, the thing I always check in a Snowflake environment is auto-suspend -- it's billed per second, so a warehouse nobody remembered to suspend, sitting idle at Large size overnight, is just burning money for nothing. I'd set a short auto-suspend window on anything that isn't under constant, steady load, and rely on auto-resume to make that invisible to users.
commonMistakes: Assuming warehouse size and multi-cluster scaling solve the same problem, when size addresses per-query speed and multi-cluster addresses concurrency
Forgetting Snowflake bills per-second for an idle-but-running warehouse, making auto-suspend a real cost control, not just a nice-to-have
Not knowing auto-resume handles bringing the warehouse back online transparently, at the cost of a brief resume latency
Thinking a bigger single warehouse automatically fixes queueing from many concurrent small queries
keyPoints: Warehouses are billed per-second based on size while running, regardless of how busy they are
auto-suspend stops billing after a configured idle period; auto-resume brings it back on demand
Warehouse size scales per-query compute (scale up); multi-cluster scales concurrency (scale out)
Multi-cluster warehouses add/remove clusters automatically based on queueing, not query size

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains per-second billing and auto-suspend/resume
Correctly distinguishes scale-up (size) from scale-out (multi-cluster)
Clarity of explanation with a concrete scenario

questions.title: Why Terraform state matters
questions.prompt: What is Terraform state actually for, why is keeping it as a local file on one engineer's laptop a real operational risk, and what does 'drift' mean in this context?
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform state (the .tfstate file) is Terraform's own record of exactly which real-world resources it created, and what their attributes were as of the last apply -- it's the only way Terraform can tell the difference between 'a resource exists but Terraform doesn't know about it' and 'a resource Terraform manages and knows the current configuration of.' Every plan and apply compares the desired configuration (the .tf files) against this state file, not directly against the cloud provider's live resources, to figure out what needs to be created, changed, or destroyed. Keeping state as a local file on one person's laptop is risky for several concrete reasons: if that laptop is lost or the file is corrupted, Terraform loses its entire record of what it manages and can no longer safely plan changes without manual recovery; two engineers working from different local state files can each believe they have the authoritative picture and issue conflicting applies; and the state file itself often contains sensitive values (like database passwords set as resource attributes) in plain text, which shouldn't be floating around on individual machines or committed to git. 'Drift' is what happens when the real infrastructure no longer matches what's recorded in state -- for example, someone manually changes a setting in the cloud console instead of through Terraform -- so the next plan shows a diff that doesn't correspond to any actual code change, just a mismatch between what Terraform believes exists and what's actually there.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain state as Terraform's memory -- without it, every apply would have no way to know what it already created versus what's new, so it would try to recreate everything from scratch every single time. The local-file risk is less about losing the file outright, though that's bad too, and more about collaboration -- if I run terraform apply from my laptop's state and a teammate runs it from theirs, we're both working from a different, out-of-sync picture of reality, and the outcome of running both can genuinely conflict or double-provision resources. That's why I treat remote state (an S3 backend with DynamoDB locking, or Terraform Cloud) as non-negotiable the moment more than one person touches the infrastructure -- it gives everyone the same source of truth and prevents two applies from running at the same time. Drift is the other thing I watch for constantly -- if someone clicks around in the Azure or AWS console and changes something Terraform manages, the next plan is going to show a diff that has nothing to do with any code change, and if I don't recognize that as drift, I might accidentally 'fix' a manual emergency change by reverting it back to the old config without realizing why it was changed.
commonMistakes: Thinking Terraform compares its config directly against live cloud resources rather than against the recorded state file
Not recognizing local state as a serious collaboration and single-point-of-failure risk once more than one person is involved
Assuming state files never contain sensitive data, when resource attributes like generated passwords can end up stored there in plain text
Confusing drift (infrastructure changed outside Terraform) with a legitimate planned change from updated .tf code
keyPoints: State is Terraform's record of what it manages and its last-known configuration
Plans/applies compare desired config against state, not directly against live infrastructure
Local state creates collaboration conflicts, loss risk, and potential secret exposure
Drift is a mismatch between real infrastructure and recorded state, usually from an out-of-band manual change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of Terraform state
Identifies concrete risks of local state
Correctly defines drift

questions.title: Bronze, silver, gold in plain terms
questions.prompt: In a medallion architecture on Databricks, what's actually different about the data at the bronze, silver, and gold layers, and why bother with three layers instead of just cleaning the raw data once and loading it straight into a reporting table?
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze holds raw data essentially as it arrived from the source -- ingested with minimal or no transformation, often with the original source schema and format preserved, plus some light metadata like an ingestion timestamp. The point of keeping it this unmodified is that it's a durable, replayable record of exactly what was received, so if a downstream transformation turns out to have a bug, the fix can be rerun from bronze without needing to re-extract from the original source system. Silver applies cleaning, conforming, and validation -- deduplication, type casting, standardizing column names, enforcing a schema, filtering out clearly bad records -- producing a queryable, trustworthy, but still fairly granular and source-system-shaped dataset. Gold is business-level, aggregated, and modeled specifically for consumption -- star-schema fact and dimension tables, or pre-aggregated metrics that map directly to how a report or dashboard actually wants to read the data. The reason for three layers instead of one is reprocessing safety and separation of concerns: if the gold-layer business logic changes (a new way of calculating a metric) or a bug is found in silver's cleaning logic, the layers below are still intact and can be reprocessed without touching the original raw ingestion, which would be far riskier and sometimes outright impossible if the source system has already deleted or rotated the original data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as three checkpoints, each with a different job. Bronze is 'did we capture exactly what the source sent us, with nothing lost or silently altered' -- it's not meant to be pretty, it's meant to be a faithful, replayable copy. Silver is 'is this data now actually trustworthy' -- types are correct, duplicates are gone, obviously bad rows are filtered, and it's something I'd be comfortable letting another engineer query directly, even if it's not shaped the way a business dashboard wants to consume it. Gold is 'is this shaped for the actual business question' -- star schema, pre-aggregated, ready for a BI tool to point at with minimal additional logic. The reason I don't just collapse all of that into one cleaning step straight into a reporting table is reprocessing risk -- if I find a bug in how I'm deduplicating records, I want to be able to fix that logic and replay silver and gold from the bronze data I already captured, rather than discovering the original source system has already purged the raw records I'd need to re-extract.
commonMistakes: Describing bronze as already cleaned, rather than raw/minimally-transformed
Thinking gold is just 'more cleaned' silver data rather than specifically business-modeled and aggregation-ready
Not recognizing reprocessing safety (being able to replay from an earlier layer) as the main reason for the layered approach
Assuming medallion architecture is Databricks-specific terminology for something that can't be applied on other platforms
keyPoints: Bronze: raw, minimally-transformed, a faithful replayable copy of the source
Silver: cleaned, deduplicated, type-cast, validated -- trustworthy but still granular
Gold: business-modeled, aggregated, consumption-ready (often a star schema)
Layering exists mainly for reprocessing safety and separation of concerns, not just aesthetics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes each of the three layers
Explains the reprocessing/separation-of-concerns rationale for layering
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Write a LAG query for month-over-month change
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against a MonthlySales table (Columns: SalesMonth DATE, TotalAmount MONEY) that returns each month's TotalAmount alongside the prior month's TotalAmount and the dollar change between them, ordered chronologically.
questions.code:
-- dbo.MonthlySales: SalesMonth DATE, TotalAmount MONEY
-- One row per calendar month, already aggregated
questions.modelAnswer: LAG(column, offset) OVER (ORDER BY ...) looks backward a given number of rows (default offset 1, meaning the immediately preceding row) within the window's ordering, and returns NULL when there is no such preceding row -- which happens naturally for the very first month in the dataset, since there's nothing before it to look back to. Because LAG is a window function, it doesn't collapse or group any rows the way an aggregate with GROUP BY would; every row from MonthlySales still appears individually in the output, just with an extra computed column. Subtracting the LAG'd value from the current row's TotalAmount in the same SELECT gives the month-over-month dollar change directly, and that NULL for the first row naturally propagates into a NULL change as well, which is the correct, honest answer since there's no prior month to compare against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for LAG(TotalAmount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) specifically because the alternative -- a self-join on SalesMonth = DATEADD(month, -1, SalesMonth) -- is more code, more fragile around month-boundary date math, and genuinely slower on a large table since it's a join instead of a single ordered pass. I'd just subtract the LAG'd value from TotalAmount in the same SELECT to get the change column directly. The one thing I always say out loud when I hand this back: the first row's PriorMonthAmount and Change will both be NULL, and that's correct, not a bug -- there's no month before the first one in the data, so there's nothing to compute a change against.
questions.example:
SELECT
    SalesMonth,
    TotalAmount,
    LAG(TotalAmount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS PriorMonthAmount,
    TotalAmount - LAG(TotalAmount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS MonthOverMonthChange
FROM dbo.MonthlySales
ORDER BY SalesMonth;
commonMistakes: Reaching for a self-join with DATEADD instead of LAG, adding unnecessary complexity and join cost
Being surprised by NULL on the first row instead of recognizing it's the expected, correct result
Forgetting the ORDER BY inside OVER() determines what 'prior' even means -- omitting or getting it wrong silently breaks the result
Trying to add a GROUP BY around a window function call unnecessarily, not realizing LAG doesn't need or want one
keyPoints: LAG(column, offset) OVER (ORDER BY ...) looks back a given number of rows in the specified order
Window functions don't collapse rows -- every input row still appears in the output
The first row in the window naturally returns NULL since there's nothing before it
Subtracting LAG's result from the current value gives the period-over-period change directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct LAG syntax with proper OVER/ORDER BY
Correctly computes the change column
Explains the first-row NULL behavior correctly

questions.title: Write a dbt staging model with a schema test
questions.prompt: Write a dbt staging model named stg_orders that selects from a raw source table using ref()/source() conventions, casts order_id and renames a few columns, and add a schema.yml snippet applying unique and not_null tests to order_id.
questions.code:
-- raw.orders columns: id (varchar), cust_id (varchar), order_dt (varchar), amt (varchar)
-- sources.yml already declares source('raw', 'orders')
questions.modelAnswer: A staging model's job is narrow and deliberate: light renaming, type casting, and maybe trivial filtering, with no business logic or joins -- that keeps a single, well-understood layer responsible for making raw source data queryable and correctly typed, before any heavier transformation happens downstream. Pulling from the raw table through source('raw', 'orders') rather than hard-coding the schema/table name is what lets dbt track lineage back to the actual source and lets source freshness checks work; referencing another dbt model (as opposed to a raw source) always goes through ref(), never a hard-coded table name, which is what lets dbt build its dependency graph and run models in the correct order. The generic tests unique and not_null on order_id encode the exact same guarantee a primary key would in a relational database, except enforced by dbt at build/test time rather than by the warehouse itself, which matters because many cloud warehouses don't actually enforce primary key constraints at the engine level.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the model itself as about as plain as dbt models get -- select from source('raw', 'orders'), cast id to an integer and rename it order_id, cast order_dt properly, rename amt to order_amount and cast it numeric. No joins, no business logic -- that all belongs in intermediate or marts models downstream. The schema.yml tests are the part I'd never skip: unique and not_null on order_id is me explicitly encoding 'this is supposed to behave like a primary key,' and running dbt test is what actually catches it the day that assumption breaks, say if the source system starts sending duplicate order IDs after an upstream change. I always point out that dbt test doesn't run automatically just because the model exists -- it has to be part of the CI pipeline or a scheduled job, or that broken assumption can sit silently unnoticed for a while.
questions.example:
-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql
SELECT
    CAST(id AS INTEGER)        AS order_id,
    CAST(cust_id AS INTEGER)   AS customer_id,
    CAST(order_dt AS DATE)     AS order_date,
    CAST(amt AS NUMERIC(10,2)) AS order_amount
FROM {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}

# models/staging/schema.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: stg_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
commonMistakes: Hard-coding the raw table's schema/name instead of using source(), breaking lineage tracking and source freshness
Putting joins or business logic into a staging model instead of keeping it to light renaming/casting
Forgetting the schema.yml tests entirely, leaving a broken uniqueness or nullability assumption to surface downstream instead of at the staging layer
Referencing another dbt model with a hard-coded table name instead of ref(), breaking dbt's dependency graph
keyPoints: Staging models do light renaming/casting only -- no joins or business logic
source() points at raw tables; ref() points at other dbt models -- both build dbt's DAG and lineage
unique/not_null are dbt's built-in generic tests, encoding a primary-key-like guarantee
Tests only run when dbt test is actually executed, typically in CI or a scheduled job

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of source() and appropriate casting/renaming
Correct schema.yml test syntax
Explains why tests matter operationally

questions.title: Write a TaskFlow DAG with automatic XCom
questions.prompt: Rewrite a two-task Airflow pipeline (extract, then load) using the TaskFlow API (@dag and @task decorators) so that the value extract returns is automatically passed to load, without manually calling xcom_push or xcom_pull.
questions.code:
from airflow.decorators import dag, task
from datetime import datetime
questions.modelAnswer: The TaskFlow API, built on @task, lets a Python function's return value automatically become an XCom value behind the scenes -- the engineer writes ordinary Python functions and ordinary function calls, and Airflow handles the XCom push and pull machinery implicitly. Calling extract() inside the DAG function and assigning its return value to a variable, then passing that variable into load(...), is enough: Airflow detects the dependency from that data flow and both pushes extract's return value to XCom and pulls it back for load automatically, which also implicitly creates the task dependency (load now depends on extract) without needing an explicit >> operator. This removes an entire class of boilerplate and a common source of bugs in classic PythonOperator-based DAGs, where forgetting to call xcom_pull with the exact right task_id and key is an easy mistake.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this the way the TaskFlow API is meant to be used -- as close to plain Python as Airflow allows. extract becomes a @task-decorated function that just returns its result like any normal function would; load becomes a @task-decorated function that takes a parameter. Inside the @dag-decorated function, I just write extracted = extract() followed by load(extracted), exactly like calling two regular Python functions in sequence. Airflow quietly handles turning that return value into an XCom entry and pulling it back out for the next task's parameter -- I never touch xcom_push or xcom_pull directly. The dependency between the two tasks also falls out automatically from that data flow; I don't need a separate >> line, because Airflow can see that load's input literally came from extract's output.
commonMistakes: Still manually calling xcom_push/xcom_pull inside TaskFlow-decorated functions, defeating the point of the API
Forgetting to actually call the @dag-decorated function at module level, which means the DAG never gets registered
Trying to pass a non-serializable Python object through the implicit XCom mechanism, which fails since XCom values must be serializable
Adding a redundant >> dependency when the data-flow call (load(extracted)) already establishes it automatically
keyPoints: @task functions can return a value directly; Airflow handles XCom push/pull automatically
Passing one task's return value into another establishes the dependency implicitly, no >> needed
The @dag-decorated function must be called at module level to actually register the DAG
XCom values still need to be serializable -- TaskFlow doesn't remove that underlying constraint

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct @dag/@task decorator usage
Correctly passes data between tasks via return value/parameter, not manual XCom calls
DAG is actually instantiated/callable at module level

questions.title: Write a MERGE statement for an upsert
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL MERGE statement that upserts rows from a staging table (#StagingCustomers) into dbo.Customers: update matching rows on CustomerID where any column differs, and insert rows that don't yet exist.
questions.code:
-- dbo.Customers(CustomerID INT PK, Name NVARCHAR(100), Email NVARCHAR(100))
-- #StagingCustomers has the same shape, freshly loaded
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE compares a target table against a source using a join condition (ON target.CustomerID = source.CustomerID) and lets a single statement branch into different actions depending on whether a match was found: WHEN MATCHED runs an UPDATE on rows that exist in both, and WHEN NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] runs an INSERT for rows that exist in the source but not yet in the target. Adding a condition to WHEN MATCHED (AND (target.Name <> source.Name OR target.Email <> source.Email)) avoids issuing a no-op UPDATE on rows that are already identical, which matters because an UPDATE still fires triggers, touches transaction log space, and can bump a LastModified-style column even when nothing actually changed. MERGE must end with a terminating semicolon -- its syntax requires one, unlike most other T-SQL statements where it's only a strong convention.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the ON clause matching on CustomerID first, since that's the natural key both tables share. For WHEN MATCHED, I wouldn't just blindly update every matched row -- I'd add a condition checking whether Name or Email actually changed, because an unconditional UPDATE on every match means I'm rewriting rows that are byte-for-byte identical to what's already there, which is wasted log activity and can trigger downstream change-tracking systems for a change that didn't really happen. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles the genuinely new customers with an INSERT. The one syntax detail I always remember because I've been burned by it before: MERGE statements require a terminating semicolon, which isn't optional the way it usually is elsewhere in T-SQL.
questions.example:
MERGE dbo.Customers AS target
USING #StagingCustomers AS source
    ON target.CustomerID = source.CustomerID
WHEN MATCHED AND (
        target.Name  <> source.Name
     OR target.Email <> source.Email
    ) THEN
    UPDATE SET target.Name = source.Name, target.Email = source.Email
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (CustomerID, Name, Email)
    VALUES (source.CustomerID, source.Name, source.Email);
commonMistakes: Omitting the change-detection condition on WHEN MATCHED, causing an unconditional UPDATE on every matched row even when nothing changed
Forgetting the terminating semicolon, which MERGE requires unlike most other T-SQL statements
Not considering WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE for rows that should be deleted/deactivated if they disappear from the source
Comparing nullable columns with <> directly without accounting for NULL, which can cause rows to be incorrectly flagged as changed or unchanged
keyPoints: MERGE joins target and source, then branches into WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED actions
Adding a change-detection condition to WHEN MATCHED avoids wasteful no-op updates
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles inserts for genuinely new rows
MERGE requires a terminating semicolon

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct MERGE syntax with proper ON clause
WHEN MATCHED includes change-detection condition
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET insert logic

questions.title: Write a recursive CTE for an org chart
questions.prompt: Given an Employees table (EmployeeID, Name, ManagerID), write a recursive CTE that returns every employee along with their management-chain depth (the CEO, with a NULL ManagerID, is depth 0).
questions.code:
-- dbo.Employees(EmployeeID INT, Name NVARCHAR(100), ManagerID INT NULL)
-- ManagerID is NULL only for the top-level employee (CEO)
questions.modelAnswer: A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member, which seeds the recursion with the base case rows (here, the employee or employees with ManagerID IS NULL, at depth 0), and a recursive member, which references the CTE's own name to join the next level -- each pass finds employees whose ManagerID matches an EmployeeID already found in the previous pass, incrementing the depth by one each time. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member against the newest batch of rows found until a pass produces zero new rows, at which point the recursion naturally terminates. Because a data error (a ManagerID loop, however unlikely) could in principle cause infinite recursion, SQL Server enforces a default MAXRECURSION limit of 100 and raises an error if that's exceeded, which can be adjusted with the MAXRECURSION hint when a genuinely deep hierarchy needs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the anchor as the CEO row -- WHERE ManagerID IS NULL -- with Depth hard-coded to 0, since that's the base case with nothing to recurse from. The recursive part joins Employees back to the CTE itself on e.ManagerID = cte.EmployeeID, which is exactly the logic of 'find the direct reports of everyone I found last pass,' and Depth + 1 tracks how far down the chain each row is. SQL Server just keeps looping that join until a pass comes back empty, which naturally happens once it's walked all the way down to the employees with no direct reports. I'd also mention MAXRECURSION explicitly in an interview, since it's a detail that shows I understand this isn't magic -- SQL Server defaults to capping recursion at 100 levels specifically to protect against infinite loops from a bad ManagerID cycle in the data, and I'd only raise that limit with OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) if I had a legitimate reason to expect a deeper hierarchy.
questions.example:
WITH OrgChart AS (
    SELECT EmployeeID, Name, ManagerID, 0 AS Depth
    FROM dbo.Employees
    WHERE ManagerID IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.EmployeeID, e.Name, e.ManagerID, oc.Depth + 1
    FROM dbo.Employees AS e
    INNER JOIN OrgChart AS oc ON e.ManagerID = oc.EmployeeID
)
SELECT EmployeeID, Name, Depth
FROM OrgChart
ORDER BY Depth, EmployeeID;
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which can silently drop legitimately duplicate-looking rows at different depths
Forgetting the anchor member entirely, leaving the recursion with no base case to start from
Not understanding why MAXRECURSION exists, or being unaware it defaults to 100 and can error out on a deep enough hierarchy
Joining the recursive member in the wrong direction (ManagerID to ManagerID instead of ManagerID to EmployeeID), breaking the parent-child walk
keyPoints: A recursive CTE has an anchor member (base case) and a recursive member joined with UNION ALL
The recursive member re-joins the CTE to itself, walking one level deeper each pass
Recursion terminates naturally when a pass returns zero new rows
SQL Server caps recursion at MAXRECURSION 100 by default to guard against infinite loops

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct anchor member
Correct recursive member and join direction
Correctly uses UNION ALL and understands MAXRECURSION

questions.title: Write a dbt incremental model
questions.prompt: Write a dbt incremental model for fct_events that only processes rows newer than what's already in the table, using the is_incremental() macro, with an append incremental strategy.
questions.code:
-- source('raw', 'events') columns: event_id, event_time, user_id, event_type
-- this.event_time refers to the already-built fct_events table within is_incremental()
questions.modelAnswer: The config block at the top sets materialized='incremental' and an incremental_strategy (append is the simplest: just insert new rows, no attempt to update or delete existing ones). is_incremental() is a Jinja macro that evaluates to false on the very first run (or any full --full-refresh run), when the target table doesn't exist yet or is being rebuilt from scratch -- in that case the whole source table is selected. On every subsequent normal run, it evaluates to true, and the WHERE clause inside the {% if is_incremental() %} block filters the source down to only rows with event_time later than the maximum event_time already present in the target table (referenced as {{ this }}), so only genuinely new rows get selected and appended. This is specifically why incremental models are far cheaper to run repeatedly on a large, append-only table than a full table rebuild would be -- the model only ever processes the new slice of data, not the entire historical dataset every single run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set materialized='incremental' with incremental_strategy='append' in the model config, since event data is naturally append-only -- nothing needs updating once an event's landed. The actual trick is the {% if is_incremental() %} block: on the very first build, or anytime someone runs --full-refresh, is_incremental() is false, so dbt just selects everything from the source and builds the table fresh. On every normal run after that, it's true, and I filter the source to event_time > (SELECT MAX(event_time) FROM {{ this }}) -- {{ this }} is dbt's way of referring to the model's own already-built table, so I'm literally asking 'give me anything newer than what's already in there.' That's the whole reason incremental exists: instead of rebuilding a potentially enormous events table from scratch every single run, each run only has to read and insert the new slice.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the is_incremental() guard entirely, which means every run re-selects and re-inserts the whole source table
Not handling the --full-refresh case, leaving no way to rebuild the table from scratch if the logic needs correcting
Using append on a dataset that actually needs updates (late-arriving corrections), when a merge strategy would be more correct
Referencing the wrong column for the incremental filter, allowing gaps or duplicate reprocessing of rows between runs
keyPoints: materialized='incremental' plus an incremental_strategy controls how new rows are merged in
is_incremental() is false on the first run or a --full-refresh, true on normal subsequent runs
{{ this }} refers to the model's own already-built table, used to find the high-water mark
append is the simplest strategy -- correct for genuinely append-only data, not for late-arriving corrections

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct incremental config and is_incremental() usage
Correct high-water-mark filter logic using {{ this }}
Understands append vs. other strategies' tradeoffs

questions.title: Write an idempotent Snowflake COPY INTO
questions.prompt: Write a Snowflake COPY INTO statement that loads all CSV files from a stage into a table, and explain why running the exact same command twice against the same stage doesn't double-load the data.
questions.code:
-- Target: raw.orders_raw
-- Stage: @raw_stage, holding CSV files with a header row
questions.modelAnswer: A basic COPY INTO names the target table, the stage/path to load from, and a FILE_FORMAT describing how to parse the files (delimiter, header handling, and so on). What makes COPY INTO naturally idempotent is Snowflake's built-in load metadata: for each stage, Snowflake keeps a record of which specific files it has already successfully loaded (tracked by file name and a checksum of its contents) for a default retention window of 64 days. Running the exact same COPY INTO again against the same stage doesn't reprocess files it already loaded -- it skips them automatically, because Snowflake recognizes them as already-ingested based on that load history, not based on anything the SQL statement itself does differently. This means the common failure mode isn't duplicate loading from re-running the same command, but the opposite: if a file is modified and re-uploaded with the exact same name, Snowflake may need FORCE=TRUE to reload it, since by default it still treats that filename as already processed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the straightforward version -- COPY INTO raw.orders_raw FROM @raw_stage with a FILE_FORMAT matching the CSVs' structure. The thing I'd actually explain, since it's the more interesting part of the question, is that I don't need to build my own dedup logic to avoid double-loading if this command accidentally runs twice -- Snowflake already tracks which files from a stage it's successfully loaded, by filename and checksum, for about 64 days by default, and it just skips anything it recognizes. Where that safety net actually bites people is the opposite scenario: if someone fixes a bad file and re-uploads it with the identical filename, Snowflake will, by default, assume it's already loaded that file and skip it again -- that's when FORCE=TRUE is actually needed, specifically to override the default skip-if-already-loaded behavior.
questions.example:
COPY INTO raw.orders_raw
FROM @raw_stage
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'CSV', SKIP_HEADER = 1, FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"')
ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
commonMistakes: Assuming re-running COPY INTO will double-load data unless custom dedup logic is added, rather than relying on Snowflake's built-in load metadata
Not knowing FORCE=TRUE exists or what it's actually for (reloading a filename Snowflake has already marked as processed)
Forgetting FILE_FORMAT entirely or mismatching it against the actual file structure, causing parse errors instead of a clean load
Assuming the load-history tracking window is permanent rather than a default ~64-day retention
keyPoints: COPY INTO is idempotent by default -- Snowflake tracks already-loaded files by name and checksum
Re-running the same COPY INTO skips files it already successfully loaded, no manual dedup needed
FORCE=TRUE overrides that skip behavior to reload a filename Snowflake has already marked as processed
Load history retention is a default window (~64 days), not indefinite

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct COPY INTO syntax with FILE_FORMAT
Correctly explains Snowflake's built-in load-tracking idempotency
Correctly explains when/why FORCE=TRUE is needed

questions.title: Resolve a git merge conflict in a dbt model
questions.prompt: You and a teammate both edited the same dbt model file on separate branches. When you try to merge your branch into main, git reports a conflict in that file. Walk through exactly how you'd resolve it, from seeing the conflict to pushing the fix.
questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
    WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
=======
    WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, CURRENT_DATE)
>>>>>>> feature/rolling-window
questions.modelAnswer: Git marks a conflict by inserting conflict markers directly into the file at every spot it couldn't automatically reconcile: <<<<<<< HEAD through ======= shows the version from the branch currently checked out, and ======= through >>>>>>> <branch-name> shows the incoming version from the branch being merged in. Resolving it means opening the file, understanding what each side was actually trying to accomplish (not just picking one side blindly), editing the file to the correct final content, and removing all three marker lines entirely -- leaving any marker in place is a syntax error in the resulting file, not just an untidy diff. Once the file reflects the intended logic, git add on that file marks the conflict as resolved, and completing the merge (continuing a merge commit, or committing directly if it was a rebase) finishes the process; the result then gets pushed like any other commit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by actually reading both sides instead of reflexively picking 'mine' or 'theirs' -- in this example, one branch hard-coded a 2026-01-01 cutoff and the other made it a rolling one-year window, and those aren't the same intent at all, so I'd want to understand which one is actually correct now, possibly by just asking the teammate who wrote the other side. Once I've decided -- let's say the rolling window is the right long-term choice -- I'd edit the file to keep just that line and delete all three conflict marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) completely; leaving even one of those in is going to break the SQL, not just look messy. Then it's git add on the resolved file, git commit to finish the merge (or git rebase --continue if I was rebasing), and push. If the conflict is something I'm not fully sure how to resolve safely -- say it touches core logic I don't fully understand -- I wouldn't guess; I'd loop in whoever wrote the other side before finalizing it.
questions.example:
-- After editing, the resolved file has NO marker lines left:
    WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, CURRENT_DATE)

-- Then:
git add models/marts/fct_orders.sql
git commit
git push
commonMistakes: Blindly accepting 'ours' or 'theirs' without understanding what each side was actually trying to do
Leaving one or more conflict marker lines in the file, which breaks the SQL rather than just looking untidy
Resolving a conflict in business logic alone without checking in with whoever wrote the other side, when the intent genuinely wasn't obvious
Forgetting git add after editing the resolved file, which leaves the conflict still marked as unresolved
keyPoints: Conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) show both versions; they must all be removed after resolving
Resolving means understanding both sides' intent, not mechanically picking one
git add marks the file resolved; commit (or rebase --continue) finishes the merge
When intent is genuinely unclear, check with the other author before finalizing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets and resolves the conflict markers
Correct git workflow (add, commit/continue, push)
Demonstrates judgment about understanding intent, not just mechanically resolving

questions.title: Run OPTIMIZE and ZORDER on a Delta table
questions.prompt: Write the Databricks SQL commands to compact the small files in a Delta table named events (fixing a 'too many small files' problem) and optimize it for queries that frequently filter on user_id.
questions.code:
-- Table: events (Delta), heavily written to in small frequent batches
-- Common query pattern: WHERE user_id = ?
questions.modelAnswer: OPTIMIZE compacts a Delta table's many small underlying Parquet files into fewer, larger files -- this matters because frequent small writes (streaming ingestion, frequent small batch jobs) tend to leave a Delta table with thousands of tiny files, and reading many small files has significant per-file overhead that hurts query performance even when the total data volume is modest. Adding ZORDER BY (user_id) to the OPTIMIZE command co-locates rows with similar user_id values physically close together within those compacted files, which lets Spark's data-skipping feature (based on each file's min/max statistics) skip reading far more files entirely when a query filters on user_id -- effectively a form of multi-dimensional physical clustering. OPTIMIZE with ZORDER rewrites data, so it's a real compute cost that should be run on a schedule (not on every single write) rather than continuously, and it's most valuable specifically on tables that are both written to frequently in small batches and read with a predictable, selective filter pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run OPTIMIZE events first just to compact the small files -- if this table's been getting small streaming or micro-batch writes, there could be thousands of tiny Parquet files sitting underneath it, and that alone is often the biggest performance drag before I even think about clustering. Then I'd add ZORDER BY (user_id) because I know the dominant query pattern filters on that column -- ZORDER physically groups rows with similar user_id values together so that when a query comes in filtering on user_id, Spark's file-level min/max statistics let it skip entire files that can't possibly contain a match, instead of scanning everything. I wouldn't run this on every single write, though -- it's a real rewrite of data and costs real compute, so in practice I'd schedule it, maybe nightly or after a batch of ingestion, not trigger it synchronously after every small append.
commonMistakes: Confusing OPTIMIZE/ZORDER with VACUUM, which instead removes old, no-longer-referenced data files rather than compacting or clustering current ones
Running OPTIMIZE after every single small write, treating it as free when it's actually a real compute cost
Choosing a ZORDER column that doesn't match the table's actual common filter pattern, getting little or no data-skipping benefit
Assuming ZORDER physically sorts the whole table globally rather than clustering similar values together within compacted files
keyPoints: OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer, larger ones, reducing per-file read overhead
ZORDER BY co-locates similar values in a column to enable Spark's file-level data skipping
OPTIMIZE/ZORDER are real compute costs -- run on a schedule, not after every write
Pick the ZORDER column based on the actual dominant filter pattern of real queries

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct OPTIMIZE syntax
Correct ZORDER BY usage and rationale
Correctly distinguishes from VACUUM and notes scheduling tradeoff

questions.title: Write a parameterized Terraform variable for multi-environment deploys
questions.prompt: Write a Terraform configuration snippet that declares a variable for environment name and uses it to name an Azure storage account consistently across dev, staging, and prod, without duplicating the resource block per environment.
questions.code:
# variables.tf and main.tf
# Need: storage account named consistently, e.g. "stdataeng<env>"
questions.modelAnswer: A variable block declares an input that the same configuration can receive different values for across environments -- the resource block itself is written once, referencing var.environment inside an interpolated name, and the actual environment-specific value is supplied externally (a .tfvars file per environment, a -var flag, or a CI pipeline variable) rather than hard-coded into the .tf files. This is the core pattern that avoids duplicating near-identical resource blocks for dev/staging/prod: one set of .tf files, multiple sets of input values, typically paired with separate state files or workspaces per environment so a plan against dev can never accidentally be applied against prod's state. A validation block on the variable (restricting allowed values to dev, staging, prod) catches a typo in the environment name at plan time rather than letting it silently create a resource with an unintended name.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd declare variable "environment" with a validation block locking it to just dev, staging, or prod -- that's a small thing but it catches a typo immediately at plan time instead of letting a misspelled environment name silently create a resource with the wrong name in production. The resource block itself only gets written once, with the storage account name built from a string interpolation like "stdataeng${var.environment}". What actually makes this safe for multiple environments isn't just the variable, though -- it's pairing it with separate state per environment, either separate .tfvars files pointed at separate remote state backends, or Terraform workspaces, so that running terraform apply against dev's variables can't possibly touch prod's actual infrastructure or state file.
commonMistakes: Writing a separate, duplicated resource block per environment instead of parameterizing one block with a variable
Not pairing environment-specific variables with separate state per environment, risking a dev apply touching prod's state
Skipping variable validation, letting a typo'd environment name silently create an incorrectly named resource
Hard-coding the environment value directly into main.tf instead of supplying it via .tfvars/CI variables
keyPoints: One set of .tf files, parameterized by variable, reused across environments
Environment-specific values come from .tfvars/-var/CI variables, not hard-coded into the resource block
Separate state per environment (workspaces or separate backends) is what actually prevents cross-environment accidents
Variable validation catches invalid/misspelled environment values at plan time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct variable declaration and interpolation into the resource
Avoids duplicating the resource block per environment
Mentions separate state per environment as the real safety mechanism

questions.title: Write a GitHub Actions job that runs dbt build in CI
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow step that installs dbt, then runs dbt build against a Snowflake target, pulling the Snowflake password from a repository secret rather than hard-coding it.
questions.modelAnswer: GitHub Actions repository secrets are encrypted values configured in the repo's settings and referenced in a workflow file as ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }} -- they're never visible in the workflow YAML itself and GitHub automatically redacts them from job logs if they ever happen to get echoed. The workflow passes that secret into the job as an environment variable (env: DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}), and dbt's profiles.yml picks it up at runtime through the env_var() Jinja function, which reads an actual OS environment variable rather than anything written in the profile file itself. This chain means the real password is never committed to the repository, never appears in the profiles.yml file checked into version control, and is only ever materialized as an environment variable inside the running CI job.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never put the actual password anywhere in profiles.yml or the workflow YAML -- it goes into the repo's Settings > Secrets as DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD, and the workflow references it as ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}, which GitHub keeps encrypted and automatically masks in logs. I'd wire that into the job step as an environment variable, and profiles.yml picks it up through env_var('DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') -- that function is dbt reaching out to the actual OS environment at runtime, not reading a value that was ever written down in a file. The thing I'd specifically avoid doing, even for a quick debug, is echoing that environment variable anywhere in a script step -- GitHub does mask known secret values in logs, but I don't want to rely on that as my only safety net, since masking isn't foolproof against every way a value could leak into output.
questions.example:
name: dbt-ci
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  dbt-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - name: dbt build
        run: dbt build --target ci
commonMistakes: Hard-coding the password anywhere in profiles.yml or the workflow file instead of using a repository secret
Forgetting to actually wire the secret into the job's env block, so env_var() has nothing to read at runtime
Echoing or printing the secret value in a debug step, risking exposure even with GitHub's log masking
