Confusing env_var() (reads an OS environment variable at runtime) with a regular Jinja variable defined inside dbt itself
keyPoints: Repository secrets are encrypted and referenced via ${{ secrets.NAME }}, never written in plain text in the workflow
Secrets are passed into the job as environment variables
profiles.yml's env_var() reads that OS environment variable at runtime, keeping the real value out of version control
Never deliberately echo a secret value in a CI log, even though GitHub masks known secrets

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of GitHub Actions secrets and env wiring
Correct understanding of env_var() in profiles.yml
States the never-hard-code/never-echo security practice

questions.title: A query got slower after an index was dropped
questions.prompt: A nightly report query that normally finishes in a few seconds has suddenly started taking several minutes. You find out a teammate dropped a nonclustered index yesterday because they thought it was unused. How would you confirm that's the cause, and what would you check before just recreating the index?
questions.code:
-- Report query filters: WHERE OrderDate BETWEEN @Start AND @End AND Status = 'Shipped'
-- Dropped index was on Orders(OrderDate, Status)
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is confirming the theory rather than assuming it: capturing the current execution plan (actual, not estimated, so the real row counts and timing show up) reveals whether the query is now doing a full table/clustered index scan where it previously used a seek -- a scan reading every row to find matches versus a seek jumping directly to the relevant rows is usually the single biggest swing in query time on a large table. Comparing that plan's operators and costs against what the query would have used with the index in place (which can sometimes be checked against a query store history if it's enabled, or simply by temporarily recreating the index) isolates the index drop as the specific cause rather than some unrelated change, like a data volume spike or a statistics update. Before blindly recreating the exact same index, it's worth checking whether 'unused' was actually correct for some other workload but wrong for this specific nightly report, and whether a slightly different index (covering additional columns the report selects, via INCLUDE) would serve this query better than simply restoring the original.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just take the teammate's word that the index was unused, and I also wouldn't just recreate it reflexively without checking first -- I'd pull the actual execution plan for the report query and look at whether it's doing a scan now where it used to do a seek on Orders filtered by OrderDate and Status. If I have query store enabled, I can literally pull up the plan from before the index was dropped and compare it side by side with today's plan, which makes the cause-and-effect obvious rather than circumstantial. Once I've confirmed the index drop is the actual cause, I'd think about whether to just recreate exactly what was dropped, or whether this is a chance to build a slightly better covering index with INCLUDE columns for exactly what this report selects -- since I'm already touching this, I might as well fix it properly instead of just undoing the mistake. And separately, I'd flag with the team that 'looks unused' needs an actual usage-stats check (sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats) before dropping anything in the future, not just intuition.
commonMistakes: Immediately recreating the exact dropped index without first confirming it's actually the cause of the slowdown
Trusting the 'looks unused' judgment without checking actual index usage statistics before any index was dropped
Looking only at estimated execution plans instead of actual plans, missing a real row-count/statistics mismatch
Missing the opportunity to build a better covering index instead of just restoring the original one
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with an actual execution plan -- look for a scan replacing what used to be a seek
Query store (if enabled) lets you directly compare the plan before and after the index drop
Don't assume 'unused' was correctly judged -- check sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats before trusting that call in the future
Consider a better covering index (with INCLUDE) rather than blindly recreating the original

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses using execution plan comparison (scan vs. seek)
Doesn't jump straight to recreating the index without verification
Considers whether a better index design should replace the original

questions.title: A dbt not_null test starts failing overnight
questions.prompt: Your nightly dbt run starts failing a not_null test on stg_customers.email that passed every night for months. Nothing in your dbt project changed. What's your diagnosis process, and what's the most likely root cause?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the dbt project itself didn't change, the most likely explanation is that the data flowing in from upstream did -- either the source system started genuinely sending NULL emails for some new category of record (a new signup flow that doesn't require email, for instance), or an upstream ETL/integration change altered how that field gets populated before it reaches this source table. The diagnosis process starts with actually looking at the failing rows: querying the staging model directly for WHERE email IS NULL and checking how many rows are affected, when they first started appearing (by created_at or a load timestamp), and whether they share some other distinguishing trait (same source system, same signup channel, same date range) that points at a specific upstream change rather than a random data quality blip. From there, the fix depends entirely on what's found: if it's a legitimate new case (guest checkouts with no email, say), the test itself might need to change to accepted_values or a where config scoping it to exclude that legitimate case, rather than assuming the data itself is simply wrong; if it's a genuine upstream bug, the right move is flagging it to whoever owns that source system rather than silently patching around bad data in dbt.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always to actually look at the data causing the failure, not guess -- I'd run a quick SELECT * FROM stg_customers WHERE email IS NULL and see how many rows, and whether they cluster around a specific time, source, or category. If the dbt project genuinely hasn't changed, the data itself changed, which usually means either a new category of legitimately-NULL record started showing up (a new signup path that doesn't collect email) or something broke upstream in how that field gets populated before it lands in my source table. I treat those two causes very differently -- if it's a legitimate new case, I'd scope the not_null test with a where clause to exclude that specific, intentional case rather than weakening the test everywhere, or switch to a more nuanced test. If it's a genuine upstream bug, I'm not going to quietly work around it in my dbt project -- I'd flag it to whoever owns that source system, because silently patching symptoms in my staging layer just hides a real data quality problem from the people who can actually fix it.
commonMistakes: Immediately loosening or removing the failing test instead of first understanding why the data actually changed
Assuming it's a dbt/project bug when nothing in the project changed, rather than investigating the upstream data itself
Not checking when the NULLs started appearing or what distinguishes those rows, missing a clear upstream-change signal
Silently patching around bad upstream data in a staging model instead of escalating a genuine upstream data quality bug
keyPoints: If the dbt project didn't change, the underlying data almost certainly did
Query the actual failing rows first -- volume, timing, and shared traits point at the real cause
A legitimate new case calls for scoping/adjusting the test, not weakening it everywhere
A genuine upstream bug should be escalated to the source system owner, not quietly worked around

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct diagnostic approach (inspect actual failing rows first)
Distinguishes legitimate new case vs. genuine upstream bug
Does not default to simply loosening the test

questions.title: An Airflow DAG is stuck with no obvious error
questions.prompt: Several tasks in a DAG are stuck in a 'queued' or 'running' state for far longer than usual, with no task failures or errors in the logs. You notice the stuck tasks are all SnowflakeSensor tasks in 'poke' mode waiting on an upstream file. What's likely happening, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A sensor in poke mode occupies a worker slot for its entire wait duration -- it runs on a worker, checks the condition, sleeps for poke_interval, wakes up, checks again, and repeats, but the worker slot is held the whole time even while it's effectively idle waiting. If enough sensors are poking simultaneously, they can exhaust the available worker slots entirely, which starves every other task in the environment (including unrelated DAGs) of a worker to actually run on -- this looks exactly like 'nothing is failing, but nothing is progressing either,' because the tasks aren't erroring, they're just queued behind a worker-slot bottleneck caused by the sensors hogging slots while waiting. The fix is switching those sensors to reschedule mode (mode='reschedule'), which releases the worker slot entirely between poke attempts instead of holding onto it idle -- the sensor becomes a lightweight, periodically-rescheduled task rather than a worker occupying a slot the entire time it's just waiting.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a classic worker-starvation pattern, and the fact that nothing's actually erroring is the tell -- if something were genuinely broken, I'd expect to see failures in the logs, not just everything queued and idle. Poke mode sensors hold a worker slot for the entire time they're waiting, even though most of that time they're doing nothing but sleeping between checks, so if enough of them are running at once, they can eat up every available worker slot and leave nothing for the rest of the DAG, or other DAGs sharing the same pool, to actually execute on. My fix would be switching those SnowflakeSensor tasks to mode='reschedule', which gives the worker slot back between each poke instead of sitting on it idle -- the sensor still checks on the same interval, it just doesn't block a worker the whole time it's waiting. I'd also double check whether a pool with a limited number of slots is specifically involved, since that narrows the blast radius of this exact problem happening again.
commonMistakes: Assuming something is broken or erroring when the actual symptom is worker-slot starvation from poke-mode sensors
Not knowing the practical difference between poke mode (holds a worker slot) and reschedule mode (releases it between checks)
Treating the fix as 'add more workers' rather than addressing the root inefficiency of poke mode for long waits
Missing that this can starve unrelated DAGs too, not just the one containing the stuck sensors, if they share the same worker pool
keyPoints: Poke mode holds a worker slot for the entire wait period, even while idle between checks
Enough simultaneous poking sensors can exhaust worker slots and starve all other tasks -- without producing any error
reschedule mode releases the worker slot between poke attempts, fixing the root cause
This can affect unrelated DAGs sharing the same worker pool, not just the DAG with the sensors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses worker-slot starvation from poke-mode sensors
Correctly recommends switching to reschedule mode
Notes the broader blast radius (other DAGs/pools affected)

questions.title: Kafka consumer lag is climbing
questions.prompt: A dashboard shows consumer lag on an order-events topic steadily climbing over the last hour, though the consumer group's instances all show as alive and not crashing. What does consumer lag actually measure, and what are the most likely explanations you'd check first?
questions.modelAnswer: Consumer lag is the difference, per partition, between the latest offset a producer has written to that partition and the latest offset the consumer group has actually committed as processed -- rising lag means production is outpacing consumption, regardless of whether anything has technically crashed. With consumers alive but lag still climbing, the most likely causes to check, roughly in order of how common they are: a sudden spike in producer volume (an upstream event burst) that simply exceeds current consumer throughput; a slow or blocking downstream dependency inside the consumer's processing logic (a database write, an external API call) that's made each message take longer to process, even though the consumer itself hasn't crashed; an uneven partition assignment or a hot partition from a skewed partitioning key, where one or two partitions are falling behind badly while others keep up fine, which average-lag dashboards can hide; and simply too few consumer instances in the group relative to the number of partitions, meaning there's a hard ceiling on how much parallel throughput the group can achieve no matter how fast each individual consumer runs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by actually defining what I'm looking at: lag is latest-produced-offset minus latest-committed-offset per partition, so climbing lag just means the topic's being written to faster than it's being consumed -- 'alive' consumers can still be too slow, that's not a contradiction. First thing I'd check is whether this is lag across every partition evenly or concentrated on one or two -- if it's concentrated, that smells like a hot partition from a skewed key, where one partition's queue is backing up while the rest of the group looks fine on an averaged dashboard. If it's spread evenly, I'd look at whether producer volume actually spiked around the same time, or whether something in the consumer's own processing logic got slower -- a downstream database or API call that used to take 10ms now taking 200ms would show up exactly like this: no crash, no error, just steadily growing lag because each message now takes longer to clear. I'd also just sanity check the math -- if there are more partitions than consumer instances in the group, there's a hard parallelism ceiling regardless of how fast any individual consumer is running.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'consumers are alive' rules out a consumer-side problem, when a slow (not crashed) consumer produces exactly this symptom
Looking only at average/aggregate lag and missing a hot-partition problem concentrated on one or two partitions
Not checking whether producer volume itself spiked, assuming the issue must be purely on the consumer side
Forgetting the hard parallelism limit when there are more partitions than active consumer instances in the group
keyPoints: Consumer lag = latest produced offset minus latest committed offset, per partition
Rising lag means production is outpacing consumption, independent of whether anything crashed
Check for producer volume spikes, slow downstream processing, hot/skewed partitions, and too few consumer instances
Partition-level lag, not just the average, reveals hot-partition problems an aggregate dashboard can hide

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines consumer lag
Lists plausible root causes covering producer, consumer, and partitioning angles
Mentions checking per-partition detail, not just aggregate lag

questions.title: The same deadlock happens every night at the same time
questions.prompt: A nightly ETL job and a nightly reporting job keep deadlocking against each other, always around the same time, always error 1205. How would you actually find the cause instead of guessing, and what are the realistic fix options?
questions.modelAnswer: The first move is capturing the actual deadlock graph rather than guessing from the error alone -- SQL Server's system_health extended event session records deadlock graphs by default, and that graph shows exactly which two queries were involved, which specific resources (which tables and even which rows/keys) each was holding and waiting on, and in what order each acquired its locks. With that information in hand, a deadlock almost always traces back to two queries touching the same rows or tables in a different order (Query A locks Table 1 then Table 2, Query B locks Table 2 then Table 1), which is what creates the circular wait. Once the actual access pattern is visible, there are a few realistic fixes depending on what's found: reordering one job's operations so both jobs touch tables in a consistent order, which removes the cycle entirely without needing any infrastructure change; simply rescheduling one job so the two no longer overlap in time at all, which is often the fastest practical fix even if it doesn't address a deeper design issue; or, if contention is from the reporting job's reads blocking the ETL job's writes (or vice versa) rather than two writers, moving the reporting job to use a snapshot-isolation read (RCSI) so its reads stop taking locks that could participate in the conflict in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start guessing at which query to rewrite -- I'd go get the actual deadlock graph first, either from the system_health extended event session (which SQL Server captures by default) or by setting up a dedicated extended event session if more detail is needed. That graph tells me exactly which two statements were involved and which specific resources each one was holding versus waiting on, which almost always reveals the same pattern: two processes locking the same tables in a different order. Once I actually see that, I've got a few real options, and which one I pick depends on what the graph shows. If it's genuinely two writers grabbing locks in opposite orders, the cleanest fix is making both jobs touch tables in the same consistent order so the cycle can't form. If it's really just unfortunate timing -- the ETL job's write window happens to overlap the reporting job's read window -- sometimes the pragmatic fix really is just rescheduling one of them so they don't run concurrently at all. And if the actual conflict is a reporting job's reads blocking an ETL job's writes, I'd look hard at moving that reporting query to RCSI so it stops taking the kind of locks that can even participate in this deadlock in the first place.
commonMistakes: Trying to fix the deadlock by guessing at query changes without first capturing the actual deadlock graph
Not knowing SQL Server's system_health session captures deadlock graphs by default, reaching for something more complicated first
Assuming a deadlock always means two writers, missing that reader/writer lock conflicts can also deadlock under default isolation
Jumping straight to 'just reschedule it' without considering whether a lock-ordering fix would more durably solve the actual root cause
keyPoints: Capture the actual deadlock graph (system_health session or a dedicated extended event) before guessing at a fix
Deadlocks usually trace back to two processes acquiring locks on the same resources in a different order
Realistic fixes: consistent lock ordering, rescheduling to avoid overlap, or RCSI if reader/writer conflict is the cause
The right fix depends on what the actual graph shows, not on assumption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes capturing and reading a deadlock graph as the first step
Correctly identifies lock-ordering as the typical root pattern
Presents realistic, differentiated fix options

questions.title: CI pipeline fails only in GitHub Actions, not locally
questions.prompt: `dbt build` runs fine on your laptop but fails in the GitHub Actions CI pipeline with an authentication error connecting to Snowflake. What's your diagnosis process, and what's the most likely cause?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the exact same dbt project authenticates successfully from a local machine but fails specifically in CI, the difference almost certainly isn't the dbt code or the Snowflake account itself -- it's how credentials reach the running process in each environment. Locally, profiles.yml's env_var('DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') likely resolves against an environment variable set in a local shell profile or .env file that's present on the laptop but was never configured as a CI secret; in GitHub Actions, if that repository secret either doesn't exist, is misspelled relative to what profiles.yml expects, or wasn't actually wired into the job's env: block, env_var() has nothing to read and the connection attempt fails with invalid or missing credentials. The diagnosis process is straightforward: check the exact secret name used in profiles.yml's env_var() call character-for-character against both the repository secret's name and the workflow YAML's env: block, since a mismatch anywhere in that three-way chain (secret name, env block key, env_var() argument) silently breaks the connection with no clear indication of which link failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption with 'works locally, fails in CI' and an auth error specifically is that it's a credentials-wiring problem, not a code or account problem -- the dbt project and the Snowflake account are identical in both places, so something about how the password actually gets to the process is different. I'd go check three things in order: does the GitHub repository secret with that exact name actually exist in Settings > Secrets; does the workflow YAML's env: block reference that secret under the exact same variable name profiles.yml expects; and does profiles.yml's env_var() call use that exact name too. It's an easy chain to break in just one spot -- someone sets up the secret as SNOWFLAKE_PWD but profiles.yml is looking for DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD, and the error you get back is a generic auth failure that doesn't obviously point at a naming mismatch. I'd fix the mismatch rather than work around it by, say, embedding a fallback value anywhere, since that would risk committing a real credential.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Snowflake account or dbt project itself is broken, rather than suspecting a credentials-wiring difference between environments
Not checking the exact secret name matches character-for-character across the GitHub secret, the workflow's env block, and profiles.yml's env_var() call
Trying to debug by printing the password value to logs to see what's wrong, risking exposing it
Assuming the local .env or shell environment variable is automatically available in CI, when it must be separately configured as a repository secret
keyPoints: 'Works locally, fails in CI' with an auth error usually points at credential-wiring, not code or account issues
Check the secret name matches exactly across: the repository secret, the workflow's env block, and env_var()'s argument
Local environment variables (shell profile, .env) don't automatically exist in CI -- they must be configured as CI secrets separately
Never debug by printing/echoing the actual secret value to logs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies credential-wiring as the likely cause, not code/account issues
Describes a concrete, systematic check of the three-way naming chain
Avoids an unsafe debugging approach (echoing secrets)

questions.title: A Snowflake query is scanning way more data than expected
questions.prompt: A query filtering a large Snowflake table on order_date runs much slower than its row count would suggest, and the Query Profile shows a full table scan with almost no partition pruning. What would you look at to explain the lack of pruning, and what fixes would you consider?
questions.modelAnswer: Snowflake automatically maintains min/max metadata per micro-partition and uses it to prune (skip) partitions that can't possibly contain matching rows for a filter -- but that pruning only works when the filter predicate is applied directly to the column as stored. Wrapping the filter column in a function, like CAST(order_date AS DATE) = '2026-11-01' here, forces Snowflake to evaluate that expression per row before it can even check it against the filter, which defeats the partition-level min/max pruning that would otherwise let it skip whole partitions outright -- this is a non-SARGable predicate, the same underlying issue that breaks index usage in other databases, just showing up as broken pruning in Snowflake instead. The fix is almost always rewriting the filter to compare the raw column directly without wrapping it in a function (order_date >= '2026-11-01' AND order_date < '2026-11-02' if order_date is actually a timestamp, or order_date = '2026-11-01' directly if it's already a DATE), and separately checking whether the table's natural insertion order already roughly aligns with order_date -- if the data arrived in a very different physical order (e.g., loaded in bulk from multiple unordered source files), even an unwrapped filter might not prune well, in which case clustering the table on order_date (via a clustering key) would be the next thing to consider.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'almost no pruning' detail is the giveaway here -- Snowflake prunes based on min/max stats on the raw stored column, and the moment I wrap that column in a function like CAST(), it has to evaluate the expression per row before it can even compare it to my filter value, so the whole partition-skipping optimization is defeated. I'd rewrite the filter to compare order_date directly without the CAST -- if it's a DATE column, just order_date = '2026-11-01'; if it's a timestamp, a half-open range like order_date >= '2026-11-01' AND order_date < '2026-11-02' instead of truncating it. If I rewrite that and pruning is still weak, my next suspicion is that the table's physical storage order just doesn't line up well with order_date -- maybe it was bulk-loaded from a bunch of files in a scrambled order -- and that's when I'd look at adding an explicit clustering key on order_date so Snowflake's background reclustering keeps similar dates physically grouped together over time.
questions.example:
-- Instead of wrapping the column in a function:
SELECT *
FROM sales.fact_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-11-01' AND order_date < '2026-11-02';
commonMistakes: Not recognizing that wrapping a filter column in a function (CAST, DATE_TRUNC, etc.) defeats Snowflake's min/max partition pruning
Assuming pruning problems always require a clustering key, without first checking whether the predicate itself is simply non-SARGable
Rewriting the filter correctly but not verifying the fix actually improved the Query Profile's pruning statistics afterward
Confusing Snowflake's automatic micro-partition pruning with an index, and looking for an index to add instead
keyPoints: Pruning requires comparing the raw stored column directly -- wrapping it in a function breaks it
A non-SARGable predicate forces per-row evaluation instead of partition-level min/max comparison
Rewrite the filter to avoid wrapping the column; verify improved pruning in the Query Profile afterward
If physical storage order still doesn't align with the filter column, a clustering key is the next lever

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the non-SARGable predicate as the root cause of broken pruning
Provides a correct rewritten filter
Considers clustering keys as a secondary fix if needed

questions.title: Terraform plan shows unexpected drift
questions.prompt: You run `terraform plan` on infrastructure nobody has intentionally changed recently, and it shows a diff for a resource's setting that you didn't touch in the .tf files. How would you figure out what's actually going on before running apply?
questions.modelAnswer: This plan output means the real infrastructure's current min_tls_version is TLS1_0, but Terraform's desired configuration says TLS1_2 -- and crucially, a plan diff doesn't by itself say whether that happened because someone (or some automated process) changed the live resource outside of Terraform, which is drift, versus whether this value was recently added or changed in the .tf code and simply hasn't been applied yet. The way to tell them apart is checking git history/blame on that specific line in the .tf file: if min_tls_version = "TLS1_2" has been sitting unchanged in the code for a while, the live resource drifted away from it, most likely from someone making a manual change directly in the Azure portal or CLI, possibly to work around an issue without realizing Terraform manages that setting; if the .tf line was just added or edited recently and never applied, this is simply a legitimate pending change, not drift at all. In Azure specifically, checking the Activity Log for that storage account around the time the value would have changed can usually identify exactly who or what changed it manually, if drift is confirmed.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd even think about running apply, I'd want to know which side moved -- did the real resource drift away from stable Terraform code, or did someone just add this setting to the .tf file and nobody's applied it yet? git log or git blame on that specific line tells me that immediately: if TLS1_2 has been sitting in the code untouched for months, the live resource is the one that moved, which means someone changed it directly in the Azure portal, probably without realizing Terraform owns that setting. If that's confirmed, I'd check Azure's Activity Log for that storage account to see exactly who or what made the change and when, since that's useful context before I just silently revert it back to TLS1_2 -- there might have been a real, if undocumented, reason someone weakened that setting, and apply would undo it without anyone being told why it mattered. Only once I understand the why would I actually run apply to bring it back in line with the intended configuration.
questions.example:
git log -p -- environments/prod/storage.tf | grep -A3 min_tls_version
# If unchanged for a while, the live resource drifted; investigate
# Azure Activity Log for that resource around the suspected change window.
commonMistakes: Running apply immediately to 'fix' the diff without first determining whether it's genuine drift or just a pending, unapplied code change
Assuming every plan diff represents drift, rather than checking whether the .tf code itself was recently and legitimately changed
Not investigating why a manual out-of-band change was made before reverting it, potentially undoing a real (if undocumented) fix
Overlooking cloud provider activity logs as a way to identify who or what made an out-of-band change
keyPoints: A plan diff alone doesn't distinguish drift from a legitimate pending code change -- check git history on that line
Drift means the live resource moved away from stable, unapplied-change-free Terraform code
Cloud provider activity logs can identify who or what made an out-of-band manual change
Understand why a manual change happened before blindly reverting it with apply

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes drift from a pending legitimate code change
Describes a concrete method to tell them apart (git history)
Investigates the why before reverting via apply

questions.title: A Delta table has thousands of tiny files and queries are slow
questions.prompt: A Delta table fed by a streaming job has grown to hold thousands of files, most well under a megabyte each, and downstream batch queries against it have gotten noticeably slower even though the total data volume hasn't grown much. What's happening, and how would you fix it without disrupting the streaming job?
questions.modelAnswer: A streaming job that commits small micro-batches frequently tends to produce one or more small Parquet files per micro-batch, and over time that accumulates into the classic 'small files problem' -- reading thousands of tiny files carries real per-file overhead (opening file handles, reading footer metadata, scheduling many small tasks) that dominates over the actual data volume once file count gets high enough, which is exactly why total data size staying flat doesn't prevent queries from getting slower as file count climbs. The fix is running OPTIMIZE on the table, which compacts many small files into fewer, appropriately-sized ones -- and this can be done without disrupting the streaming job at all, since OPTIMIZE operates on existing committed data and doesn't block or interfere with new micro-batch writes continuing to land; it's typically scheduled to run periodically (hourly or nightly, depending on write volume) rather than continuously. For an ongoing streaming source like this, enabling Delta's auto-optimize/auto-compaction features (where supported) can also reduce how often a large manual OPTIMIZE catch-up is needed, by opportunistically compacting small files as part of the write path itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the textbook small-files problem, and streaming is almost always the source of it -- each micro-batch commits its own file or files, so a job running every few seconds or minutes for weeks ends up with thousands of tiny files even if the actual data volume is modest. The per-file overhead of opening and reading metadata for thousands of small files adds up to real query latency, separate from the actual data size. The good news is the fix doesn't touch the streaming job at all -- I'd just run OPTIMIZE on the table on a schedule, maybe hourly, and it compacts the existing small files into fewer, properly-sized ones without blocking or interfering with new micro-batches continuing to land. If this table is going to keep getting high-frequency small writes indefinitely, I'd also look at enabling auto-optimize/auto-compaction on it, which does some of that compaction opportunistically as part of the write path itself, reducing how bad the small-files buildup gets between scheduled OPTIMIZE runs.
commonMistakes: Assuming slow queries mean the data volume grew, missing that file count (not size) is the actual driver of the slowdown
Thinking OPTIMIZE would need to pause or interfere with the streaming job, rather than running independently on committed data
Running OPTIMIZE only once reactively instead of scheduling it regularly for an ongoing streaming source
Not considering auto-optimize/auto-compaction as a way to reduce the problem's recurrence between manual OPTIMIZE runs
keyPoints: Frequent streaming micro-batches commit small files, accumulating into the classic small-files problem
Per-file overhead, not total data volume, drives the slowdown as file count climbs
OPTIMIZE compacts files without disrupting ongoing streaming writes -- schedule it periodically
Auto-optimize/auto-compaction can reduce recurrence for an ongoing high-frequency streaming source

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the small-files problem from streaming micro-batches
Correctly recommends OPTIMIZE without disrupting the streaming job
Mentions scheduling/auto-compaction for ongoing prevention

questions.title: Star schema basics: fact grain and dimensions
questions.prompt: What does the 'grain' of a fact table actually mean, why does getting it wrong (mixing two different grains in one fact table) cause real problems, and how do dimension tables relate to it in a basic star schema?
questions.modelAnswer: The grain of a fact table is the precise definition of what one single row in that table represents -- for example, 'one row per line item on an order' is a different, finer grain than 'one row per order,' and both are different again from 'one row per customer per day.' Every measure (quantity, amount, and so on) in the fact table has to be true at exactly that grain, and every foreign key to a dimension has to also be meaningful at that grain. Mixing two grains in one fact table -- say, some rows representing an individual order line and other rows representing an order-level total, both stored together -- breaks aggregation silently: summing the Amount column now double-counts or miscounts, because some rows represent a part and others represent the whole, and nothing in the schema itself prevents that from happening or flags it as wrong. Dimension tables in a basic star schema hold the descriptive context (customer details, product details, calendar dates) that the fact table's foreign keys point at; each dimension has its own key and attributes, and because the fact table sits at the center with a foreign key to each surrounding dimension, that's exactly the 'star' shape the schema is named for -- the fact table should never contain, say, a customer's name directly, only a foreign key to the Customer dimension that holds that name.
questions.professionalAnswer: Grain is the single most important decision in designing a fact table, and I'd define it very literally: it's the answer to 'what does exactly one row in this table mean.' If I pick 'one row per order line,' every measure in that table -- quantity, line amount -- has to be true at the line level, not the order level. The actual damage from getting this wrong shows up quietly: if I accidentally mix some rows that represent a whole order's total with other rows that represent individual line items, and someone just runs SUM(Amount) without knowing that, they're going to double-count or get a nonsensical total, and there's nothing structurally stopping that mistake from happening again later. Dimensions are the supporting cast around that fact table -- Customer, Product, Date -- each with its own key, and the fact table only ever references them by foreign key, never by duplicating their descriptive attributes directly into the fact rows. That's the actual 'star' -- one fact table at the center, dimension tables radiating out around it, each joined by a simple foreign key relationship.
commonMistakes: Not being able to state the grain of a fact table in one precise sentence before building it
Mixing two different grains in the same fact table, silently breaking SUM() and other aggregates for anyone querying it later
Storing descriptive attributes (like a customer's name) directly in the fact table instead of in a dimension referenced by foreign key
Treating grain as a minor detail rather than the foundational design decision that everything else in the fact table depends on
keyPoints: Grain = the precise definition of what one row in a fact table represents
Every measure and foreign key in the fact table must be true at that exact grain
Mixing grains in one fact table silently breaks aggregation (double-counting or miscounting)
Dimensions hold descriptive context; the fact table references them by foreign key, forming the star shape

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines grain with a precise example
Explains the concrete damage from mixed grain
Correctly describes the fact/dimension relationship

questions.title: Lakehouse vs. warehouse in Fabric: picking the engine
questions.prompt: In Microsoft Fabric, you can store the same underlying Delta data and query it through either a Lakehouse (Spark-based) or a Warehouse (T-SQL-based) item. At a basic level, what actually determines which one a team should default to for a given workload?
questions.modelAnswer: A Fabric Lakehouse exposes Spark as the primary engine (notebooks, PySpark, Spark SQL) and is organized around files and folders alongside managed Delta tables, which makes it the natural fit for data engineering work that involves heavier transformation logic, semi-structured data, or Python/Spark-native processing -- the kind of work a data engineering team typically owns. A Fabric Warehouse is a full T-SQL engine with transactional guarantees and a relational-database feel (stored procedures, multi-table transactions), which makes it the natural fit for BI and analytics teams that think in T-SQL and need full DML support with ACID transactional consistency across multiple statements. Both ultimately store data as Delta Parquet underneath and in Fabric's OneLake, so this isn't a storage-format decision at all -- it's purely about which compute engine and language the team actually working with the data is most comfortable and productive in, and which one supports the specific operations (complex Spark transformations versus full T-SQL DML and stored procedures) that workload actually needs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as a 'who's touching it and what are they comfortable with' question rather than a performance question, because under the hood it's largely the same Delta data in OneLake either way. If the team doing the work lives in notebooks, writes PySpark, and needs to do heavier, programmatic transformation logic or handle messier semi-structured data, Lakehouse is the natural fit -- that's the data engineering default. If the team is BI-oriented, thinks in T-SQL, wants real stored procedures and full multi-statement transactional DML, Warehouse is the better fit -- that's usually the analytics/BI engineering default. I'd also mention Shortcuts and Direct Lake as the reason this choice isn't as locked-in as it sounds -- Fabric's architecture is built so a Warehouse-preferring team can still read Lakehouse-managed Delta tables without copying the data, which softens the cost of picking 'wrong' for one workload early on.
commonMistakes: Treating Lakehouse vs. Warehouse as a storage-format decision, when both sit on the same underlying Delta/OneLake storage
Assuming one is unconditionally faster or better than the other, rather than recognizing it's about engine/language fit for the team and workload
Not knowing Shortcuts/Direct Lake let data be read across both without duplicating it, softening the cost of the initial choice
Picking Warehouse for heavy Spark-native transformation work just because it 'sounds more like a database,' ignoring what the actual workload needs
keyPoints: Lakehouse = Spark-based engine, natural for data engineering/notebook-based transformation work
Warehouse = T-SQL engine with full transactional DML, natural for BI/analytics teams
Both store data as Delta in OneLake underneath -- this is an engine choice, not a storage choice
Shortcuts/Direct Lake let data be accessed across both without duplication, reducing lock-in risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the decision as engine/team fit, not storage
Correctly characterizes Lakehouse and Warehouse use cases
Mentions Shortcuts/Direct Lake reducing the cost of the choice

questions.title: Why idempotent writes matter in a pipeline
questions.prompt: What does it mean for a pipeline's write step to be idempotent, and why does that property matter specifically for how safely a failed job can be retried?
questions.modelAnswer: A write is idempotent when running it two or more times with the same input produces the same end result as running it exactly once -- no duplicated rows, no double-counted totals, nothing different about the final state regardless of how many times that same write actually executed. This matters enormously for retry safety: pipelines fail for all sorts of transient reasons (a network blip, a timeout, a worker getting killed mid-run), and the standard operational response is simply to retry the failed job -- but a retry only has that simple answer if re-running the write is actually safe. A plain INSERT appending new rows is the classic non-idempotent example: if the job fails after some rows were already written but before it reported success, a naive retry re-inserts those same rows again, silently duplicating data. Common idempotent patterns include a MERGE/upsert keyed on a natural identifier (re-running it just produces the same final rows, matched and updated rather than duplicated), deleting a specific partition and rewriting it fully before inserting (so a retry just redoes the same delete-then-insert for that one partition with the same end state), or writing with an explicit, deterministic batch/dedup key the destination enforces uniqueness on.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of idempotency as the property that makes 'just retry it' an actually safe answer instead of a risky one. Jobs fail for mundane reasons all the time -- a timeout, a worker dying, a network hiccup -- and operationally, the easiest and most common response is to rerun the failed job. If the write step is a plain append-only INSERT, though, and the job failed partway through after some rows already landed, a retry duplicates those rows, and now I've got a data quality problem nobody's actively watching for until a report looks wrong. If instead the write is a MERGE keyed on the natural ID, rerunning it after a partial failure just re-matches and re-applies the same final state -- no duplicates, because the operation is defined in terms of 'end up in this state' rather than 'append whatever comes in.' The other pattern I use a lot for batch loads is delete-the-partition-then-insert -- if I always fully delete and rewrite a specific partition (like a single day), retrying that operation after a failure just redoes the same delete-and-rewrite and lands in the identical end state, regardless of how many times it actually ran.
commonMistakes: Assuming a plain append-only INSERT is safe to retry, when a partial failure before success is reported can duplicate rows
Not recognizing that idempotency is specifically what makes automatic/simple retry logic safe
Thinking idempotency only matters for streaming pipelines, when it's just as critical for batch loads
Confusing idempotency with exactly-once delivery guarantees from a messaging system, when it's a property of the write logic itself, independent of the transport
keyPoints: Idempotent write: running it multiple times with the same input produces the same end state as running it once
This is what makes simple retry-on-failure operationally safe for transient job failures
Plain append-only INSERTs are the classic non-idempotent failure mode, risking duplicates on retry
MERGE/upsert and delete-partition-then-insert are common idempotent write patterns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines idempotency for a write operation
Explains why it enables safe retries
Gives concrete idempotent write patterns

questions.title: Partition pruning, at a basic level
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what is partition pruning, why does it make such a large practical difference on a big table, and what has to be true about a query's filter for pruning to actually kick in?
questions.modelAnswer: Partitioning splits a large table's data into physically separate chunks based on the value of one or more columns -- commonly a date column, so all of a given day's or month's data lives together as its own physical unit. Partition pruning is the query engine recognizing, before it reads any actual data, that a query's filter condition makes certain partitions entirely irrelevant, and skipping them completely rather than reading and then discarding their rows -- the engine only touches data in partitions that could possibly contain a matching row. The practical impact is large because it turns a query's cost from scanning the whole table down to scanning only the relevant slice -- a query asking for one day's data out of three years of daily-partitioned history can, with effective pruning, read roughly 1/1000th as much data as it otherwise would. For pruning to actually trigger, the filter has to directly reference the partitioning column in a way the engine can statically evaluate against partition boundaries -- filtering on a literal date range on the partitioning column works cleanly, but wrapping that column in a function or comparing it indirectly through a join to another table (rather than a direct, evaluable predicate) can prevent the engine from recognizing which partitions are safe to skip, forcing it to fall back to scanning everything.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain pruning as the engine deciding what not to read before it reads anything at all. If a table's partitioned by date and I filter for one specific day, a well-behaved engine recognizes that every other day's partition simply cannot contain a matching row and skips reading those partitions entirely -- it's not reading them and filtering afterward, it's never touching them in the first place. That's why the performance difference is so dramatic on a big table: instead of scanning years of history, I might only ever touch one day's worth of data. The part I always flag, though, is that this only works if the filter is written in a way the engine can actually evaluate against partition boundaries directly -- the same non-SARGable problem that breaks Snowflake's micro-partition pruning applies here too. Wrap the partitioning column in a function, or only reach it indirectly through a join rather than a direct predicate, and pruning quietly stops working, and the only symptom you'll see is a slower-than-expected query with no obvious error.
commonMistakes: Describing pruning as filtering after reading data, rather than skipping irrelevant partitions before any data is read
Not connecting pruning to the same non-SARGable-predicate problem that breaks index/micro-partition pruning elsewhere
Assuming any filter on the partitioning column automatically triggers pruning, regardless of how it's written
Underestimating how large the practical performance impact can be on a table with many partitions
keyPoints: Partitioning splits table data into physically separate chunks by a column's value, commonly date
Pruning means the engine skips irrelevant partitions entirely before reading any data from them
The performance impact is large because the query scans only a slice of the table, not the whole thing
Pruning requires a directly evaluable predicate on the partitioning column -- wrapping it in a function can disable pruning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines partition pruning and how it differs from post-read filtering
Explains the magnitude of practical performance impact
Correctly states what breaks pruning (non-evaluable predicates)

questions.title: Designing a basic bronze-silver-gold pipeline
questions.prompt: A mid-size retailer's platform team wants a straightforward Databricks pipeline that takes raw daily sales CSV exports and makes them available as a clean, business-ready sales-by-store-by-day table for a BI dashboard. Walk through how you'd structure that across bronze, silver, and gold, including what happens at each layer and why.
questions.modelAnswer: At bronze, the raw CSV files are ingested essentially as-is into a Delta table, with minimal transformation -- maybe just adding an ingestion timestamp and the source file name as metadata columns -- and every column is typically kept as a string or loosely typed to avoid rejecting a row just because of a type mismatch at this earliest stage; the entire point is capturing a faithful, replayable copy of exactly what arrived, so that any downstream bug can be fixed and reprocessed from here without re-pulling from the original export. At silver, the bronze data gets properly typed (dates parsed, amounts cast to numeric), deduplicated (CSV re-exports or retries can produce overlapping rows), validated against basic sanity rules (rejecting or quarantining rows with a negative sale amount or a missing store ID, for instance), and conformed to consistent naming -- the result is a trustworthy, still fairly granular, line-item-level sales table that other engineers could query directly and trust. At gold, that silver data gets aggregated to the actual business grain the dashboard needs -- one row per store per day, summing sale amounts and counts -- and typically joined against a Store dimension to add business-friendly attributes like region or store name, producing a table shaped exactly for how the BI tool will query it. The reason to keep these as three separate, physically materialized layers rather than one big transformation is reprocessing safety: if the aggregation logic in gold needs to change, it can be rebuilt from silver without re-deduplicating or re-validating anything; if a data quality bug is found in silver's validation logic, it can be reprocessed from bronze without needing the original CSV exports to still exist anywhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this the way I'd actually build it. Bronze is the ingestion job pulling in the daily CSV exports into a Delta table pretty much untouched -- I'd keep most columns as strings at this stage on purpose, since the goal here isn't correctness yet, it's just making sure I've durably captured exactly what came in, with an ingestion timestamp and source filename so I can always trace a row back to which file it came from. Silver is where I'd actually earn the 'trustworthy' label -- parse dates properly, cast amounts to numeric, dedupe anything that looks like a re-exported file landed twice, and quarantine or reject anything clearly broken, like a negative sale amount or a missing store ID, rather than silently letting it flow through. Gold is where I'd actually build what the dashboard wants: group by store and day, sum the sale amounts, join in the store dimension for region and store name, and land that as its own table shaped exactly for the BI tool to query with minimal extra logic on their end. If I had to pick one reason for keeping these as three separate materialized layers instead of doing it all in one big transformation, it's that each layer gives me a safe place to reprocess from if something downstream needs to change or something upstream turns out to have been wrong -- I'm not stuck re-pulling the original CSVs just because my aggregation logic in gold needed a fix.
commonMistakes: Collapsing bronze and silver into one step, losing the ability to replay from a truly untouched copy of the source data
Doing the business-level aggregation (store/day grain) too early, in silver instead of gold, mixing concerns
Not quarantining or flagging clearly bad rows at silver, letting obviously invalid data flow all the way to the BI-facing gold table
Keeping bronze strongly typed, risking row rejection at ingestion time for a type mismatch that should be handled downstream instead
keyPoints: Bronze: raw CSV ingested nearly as-is, loosely typed, with ingestion metadata -- a faithful, replayable copy
Silver: properly typed, deduplicated, validated -- trustworthy but still at a granular, line-item grain
Gold: aggregated to the business grain (store/day), joined with dimensions, shaped for the BI tool
Three separate materialized layers exist specifically for reprocessing safety when logic changes or bugs are found

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what happens and why at each of the three layers
Correctly identifies the business grain and dimension join at gold
Explains the reprocessing-safety rationale for the layered design

deepDive.heading: Handling late-arriving or corrected daily files
deepDive.content: A realistic follow-up a principal-track candidate should be ready for: what happens if yesterday's store export arrives late, or a store resends a corrected file for a day already processed? The bronze layer should treat ingestion as append-only and tagged with both the business date the file represents and the actual ingestion timestamp, so a late or corrected file for day X doesn't get confused with day X's original file -- both exist in bronze, distinguishable by ingestion time. Silver's job then becomes picking the right version to carry forward: a common pattern is deduplicating within silver by business date and store, keeping only the latest ingestion for that combination (or explicitly unioning corrections as an override), rather than assuming one file per day arrives exactly once, on time, and never needs revision.

deepDive.heading: Why gold shouldn't be the only place reprocessing happens
deepDive.content: A tempting shortcut is to do all the real work in one flat transformation straight from bronze to a dashboard-ready table, skipping a materialized silver layer entirely to save build time. The problem shows up the first time a validation rule in the 'cleaning' logic needs to change -- without a materialized, trustworthy silver layer sitting in between, fixing that rule means re-running the entire pipeline from bronze through to the business aggregation in one pass, conflating two genuinely different kinds of change (data quality rules vs. business aggregation logic) into one brittle, harder-to-reason-about job. Keeping silver as its own real table is what lets each of those concerns evolve and get fixed independently.

questions.title: Leaving a code review comment on a small technical choice
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's pull request for a new dbt model, and you'd have written one part of it differently -- they used a nested subquery where you think a CTE would be clearer, and they hard-coded a date filter you think should be a variable. Neither is wrong, exactly. How do you phrase these in your review comments?
questions.modelAnswer: A useful review comment on a stylistic or non-blocking preference distinguishes clearly, in its own wording, between 'this is a bug' and 'this is a suggestion' -- phrasing like 'Nit:' or 'Non-blocking suggestion:' up front signals immediately that the comment isn't gating approval, which respects both the author's time and their ownership of the implementation detail. The comment itself should explain the reasoning, not just assert a preference: 'a CTE named something like recent_orders here might read more clearly than the nested subquery, since it names the intermediate step' gives the author something to evaluate and agree or disagree with on its merits, rather than 'use a CTE instead' which reads as a directive with no stated rationale. For the hard-coded date, the underlying concern (this value will probably need to change again, and a hard-coded literal buried in a WHERE clause is easy to miss next time) is worth raising because it's a maintainability point, not pure style -- but it's still appropriate to ask rather than assert: 'is this date likely to change again soon? if so, might be worth pulling it into a variable' invites a conversation rather than demanding a specific fix the author might have context the reviewer doesn't.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag both as suggestions, not blockers, and say so explicitly so there's no ambiguity about whether they're gating my approval. For the subquery, I'd write something like 'Nit: I think a named CTE here would read a bit more clearly than the nested subquery, since it'd give this intermediate step an actual name -- not blocking, just a readability thought.' I'm giving my reasoning, not just a preference, so they can weigh it and push back if they disagree. For the hard-coded date, I'd frame it as a question rather than a correction, because I don't actually know their full context: 'is this date likely to need updating again soon? if so, might be worth pulling it into a variable so it's easier to find next time.' That phrasing leaves room for them to say 'actually, this is a one-time backfill, it's fine as a literal' -- which might be completely true, and I wouldn't have known that without asking instead of asserting.
commonMistakes: Phrasing a stylistic preference as a directive ('use a CTE') without explaining the reasoning behind it
Not distinguishing, in the comment itself, between a blocking issue and a non-blocking suggestion
Asserting a fix for the hard-coded value instead of asking a question that accounts for context the reviewer might not have
Letting personal style preference block a PR's approval when the code is correct and the concern is genuinely non-blocking
keyPoints: Explicitly label a non-blocking comment as a suggestion, not a requirement, so the author isn't left guessing
Explain the reasoning behind a stylistic preference instead of just asserting it
Frame a maintainability concern as a question when you might be missing context the author has
Respect the author's ownership of implementation details that are genuinely a matter of preference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes blocking vs. non-blocking feedback in phrasing
Explains reasoning rather than just asserting a preference
Shows respect for the author's context and ownership

questions.title: Receiving a bluntly worded review comment
questions.prompt: A senior engineer leaves a comment on your pull request that reads: 'This whole approach is wrong, you should have used a window function instead of this loop.' They're probably right about the technical point, but the tone stings. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: The professionally useful move is separating the technical content of the comment from its tone, and responding to the content, because getting defensive about phrasing in the review thread itself tends to escalate rather than resolve anything, and it doesn't actually get the PR any closer to being merged. A reasonable reply acknowledges the technical point directly -- 'you're right, a window function would avoid the loop entirely, let me rework this' -- which shows the ability to accept correction gracefully and signals the review process is working as intended, even when the delivery wasn't especially diplomatic. If the tone is a recurring pattern rather than a one-off, that's worth raising separately and privately with that engineer (or, if it continues, with a manager) rather than litigating it in the PR thread itself, since a public comment thread on a specific PR is the wrong venue for addressing a communication-style concern, and doing it there risks turning a straightforward technical fix into an unnecessary conflict.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, my first instinct in the moment might be to feel a little stung, but I'd deliberately not respond to that in the thread -- I'd just respond to the actual technical point, because that's the part that matters for getting the PR merged. Something like 'good catch, a window function does avoid the loop entirely -- updating now' handles it cleanly: it shows I can take direct feedback without getting defensive, and it keeps the thread focused on the code instead of turning into something about tone. If this is a one-off, I'd genuinely let it go -- not every comment needs to be delivered gently, and getting the correct feedback matters more than how it was phrased. If I noticed this specific person consistently writes feedback this way across multiple PRs, that's a conversation I'd have with them directly and privately, not in a comment thread, because a PR discussion isn't the right venue to address someone's communication style, and doing it there would make a simple technical fix into something much bigger than it needs to be.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or arguing about tone in the PR comment thread instead of addressing the technical point
Letting a stinging tone prevent acknowledging a correct technical point
Escalating a one-off blunt comment immediately to a manager instead of handling it directly first
Addressing a pattern of poor communication style publicly in a PR thread rather than privately and directly
keyPoints: Separate the technical content from the tone, and respond to the content
Acknowledging being wrong gracefully is a professional strength, not a weakness
A PR comment thread is the wrong venue to address a tone/communication-style concern
A recurring pattern (not a one-off) is worth raising privately and directly, escalating only if it continues

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds to the technical substance rather than the tone
Shows maturity in accepting correction
Appropriately separates addressing a tone pattern from the PR thread itself

questions.title: Knowing when to ask for help
questions.prompt: You've been stuck for two hours trying to figure out why a dbt model is producing duplicate rows that shouldn't be possible given the join logic. What's your process before asking a teammate for help, and at what point do you actually ask?
questions.modelAnswer: Before escalating, the useful first step is making the problem small and concrete rather than staying stuck at the level of 'something is wrong somewhere in this model' -- isolating exactly which join is introducing the duplication (by running each join's result set independently and checking row counts at each step) narrows the actual source dramatically, and often surfaces the answer directly, like a join column that isn't as unique as assumed. Checking recent changes (git log/blame on the model and any upstream models it depends on) can reveal whether something nearby actually changed recently, versus this being a long-standing behavior nobody noticed until now. The right time to actually ask for help isn't 'the moment it gets hard' or 'only after exhausting every possible avenue for hours more' -- it's once independent investigation has produced a specific, well-formed question rather than a vague one: 'I isolated the duplication to this join against the Customer dimension -- it looks like Customer has multiple active rows per CustomerID, which I didn't expect given the SCD logic. Does that match what you'd expect, or is something off upstream?' is something a teammate can engage with productively in two minutes, versus 'my query is giving me dupes, can you help' which forces them to redo the entire diagnosis from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd ask anyone, I'd narrow this down myself -- run each join independently and check if row counts jump at a specific step, since that tells me immediately which join is actually introducing the duplication instead of leaving me guessing at the whole query. I'd also check git history on the model and anything upstream it depends on, since if something changed recently, that's probably directly relevant. Two hours stuck isn't inherently too long or too short on its own -- what actually matters to me is whether I've made the question specific. If after that digging I've found 'this join against the Customer dimension is where duplicates appear, and it looks like Customer unexpectedly has multiple active rows per ID,' that's the point where I'd go ask, because now I'm handing a teammate a concrete, answerable question instead of 'my query's broken, help.' I'd rather ask a good, specific question after an hour of real digging than either burn a whole day stuck on something a five-minute conversation would have resolved, or interrupt someone with a vague problem I hadn't actually tried to narrow down myself first.
commonMistakes: Asking for help immediately with a vague description before doing any independent narrowing of the problem
Staying stuck for an excessive amount of time out of reluctance to ask, burning far more time than a timely question would have cost
Not checking recent changes (git history) as an easy first step that often reveals the actual cause directly
Framing the eventual question too broadly ('my query is broken') instead of specifically ('I isolated it to this join')
keyPoints: Narrow the problem independently first -- isolate which specific step is causing the issue
Check recent changes (git history) on the model and its upstream dependencies
The right time to ask is once the question is specific, not purely based on elapsed time
A specific, well-formed question respects a teammate's time far more than a vague one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes concrete independent troubleshooting steps before escalating
Identifies specificity (not just time elapsed) as the right trigger to ask
Shows balance between self-reliance and timely escalation

questions.title: Getting paged for a failed nightly pipeline
questions.prompt: You're the on-call engineer and get paged at 11pm because the nightly order-pipeline DAG failed. Walk through what you actually do, start to finish, including what you'd communicate and to whom.
questions.modelAnswer: The first step on getting paged is acknowledging the page itself promptly, which simply confirms someone is actively on it and stops any escalation chain from paging a second person unnecessarily. Next is actually looking at what failed and why -- the specific task, its logs, and the error message -- rather than jumping straight to a fix, since a quick look often distinguishes between a transient issue (an upstream source was briefly unavailable, a timeout) that's safe to simply retry, versus a genuine logic or data problem that a blind retry won't resolve and might make worse. If it's a straightforward, safe retry -- say, a known-flaky external API call -- retrying and confirming the DAG completes successfully is often the end of it, with a brief note left for the team the next morning about what happened and that it was handled. If it's not a safe retry -- the root cause is unclear, the data might be genuinely bad, or fixing it incorrectly at midnight risks making things worse -- the better move is: not force an incomplete understanding into a fix; communicate the actual status (to whichever channel the team uses for incident status) honestly, including what is and isn't known yet; and if downstream consumers depend on this pipeline's output being ready by a specific time, flag that the data may be late or incomplete, rather than silently hoping no one notices. Writing down what happened afterward, even briefly, matters regardless of whether the fix was simple or complex, since the next on-call engineer (or your future self) benefits from that record the next time something similar happens.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing, I'd acknowledge the page immediately, just so the system knows someone's actually on it and doesn't escalate further. Then I'd actually go look -- which task failed, what the error says, whether this looks like a one-off transient issue or something deeper. If it looks transient, like a flaky upstream API that's failed before, I'd just retry the task and watch it complete, then leave a short note for the team the next morning saying what happened and that it resolved on retry -- no need to wake anyone else up for that. If it's not obviously transient -- say the error points at a real data or logic problem I don't fully understand at 11pm -- I wouldn't force a fix I'm not confident in just to make the page go away. I'd post an honest status update wherever the team tracks incidents, something like 'order pipeline failed, root cause isn't clear yet, data will likely be late, I'll pick this back up with fresh eyes in the morning unless someone wants to jump in now,' and if I know specific downstream consumers depend on this data being ready by a certain time, I'd flag that directly to them too rather than letting them find out the data's stale on their own. Either way, I'd write a short note on what happened before I go back to bed, because whoever's on call next time this flakes will want that context.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a fix or retry without actually reading the error/logs to understand what happened first
Blindly retrying a genuinely broken pipeline instead of distinguishing a transient issue from a real logic/data problem
Forcing an uncertain fix at midnight rather than honestly communicating status and picking it back up with fresh eyes
Not proactively flagging downstream consumers whose data will be late or incomplete as a result of the failure
keyPoints: Acknowledge the page promptly before investigating
Distinguish a safe-to-retry transient issue from a genuine logic/data problem before acting
Communicate honest status, including uncertainty, rather than forcing a fix you're not confident in
Proactively notify downstream consumers who depend on the affected data, and leave a written record afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sensible, ordered incident-response process
Distinguishes transient retry from genuine problem requiring caution
Addresses communication to the team/downstream consumers appropriately

questions.title: Documenting a pipeline you just built
questions.prompt: You just finished building a new data pipeline that nobody else has context on yet. What do you actually write down, and why does 'the code is the documentation' fall short here?
questions.modelAnswer: 'The code is the documentation' falls short because code answers 'what does this do, mechanically,' but it rarely answers the questions someone actually needs answered during an incident at 2am: why was it built this way instead of an obvious alternative, what does it depend on upstream, who to contact if a specific failure happens, and what the expected normal behavior even looks like so an abnormal one is recognizable. A useful writeup for a new pipeline typically covers: a short description of what it does and why it exists (the business purpose, not just the mechanics); its upstream dependencies and expected schedule/timing, so someone can tell at a glance whether a delay is itself a symptom of a problem; common failure modes already encountered during development and how to resolve each one, which turns a 2am guessing session into a two-minute lookup; and who owns it or who to escalate to if the documented failure modes don't cover what's actually happening. This doesn't need to be a lengthy formal document -- a runbook-style README living next to the pipeline's code, kept current as the pipeline evolves, is usually enough, and 'kept current' matters as much as writing it in the first place, since a stale runbook that describes an old version of the pipeline can be actively misleading.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write a short runbook-style README right next to the pipeline code, not a long formal doc nobody will read. It covers what the pipeline does and why it exists in plain terms, what it depends on upstream and when it's supposed to run, any failure modes I already hit while building it and exactly how I fixed each one, and who to page or message if something goes wrong that isn't already covered. The reason I don't just rely on the code being self-explanatory is that code tells you how something works, not why it was built that way or what normal versus abnormal looks like from the outside -- someone debugging this at 2am doesn't want to reverse-engineer my logic from scratch, they want to know in thirty seconds whether what they're seeing is a known issue with a known fix. I'd also make a point of actually updating that README the next time I touch the pipeline, because a stale runbook that describes how it used to work is worse than no runbook at all -- it actively misleads whoever trusts it.
commonMistakes: Assuming well-written code is sufficient documentation on its own, without capturing the why, dependencies, and failure modes
Writing an overly long, formal document that's unlikely to actually get read during an incident
Not documenting known failure modes encountered during development, forcing the next person to rediscover them from scratch
Writing documentation once and never updating it, letting it go stale and become actively misleading
keyPoints: Code explains mechanics, not why, dependencies, or what normal/abnormal behavior looks like
Document purpose, upstream dependencies/timing, known failure modes and fixes, and ownership/escalation contact
A concise runbook-style README is usually sufficient -- doesn't need to be a lengthy formal document
Keeping documentation current matters as much as writing it -- stale docs can actively mislead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why code alone is insufficient documentation
Lists the specific, useful content a runbook should include
Notes the importance of keeping documentation current

questions.title: Explaining a delay to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: A marketing manager is expecting a new dashboard metric by Friday, but you've discovered the source data has an inconsistency that needs to be resolved first, pushing the timeline to the following Wednesday. How do you explain this to them?
questions.modelAnswer: The useful structure for this kind of conversation is leading with the practical impact and the new timeline, not with the technical details of the discovery, because a non-technical stakeholder's actual question is 'when will I have this, and should I plan around a delay' -- burying that answer under an explanation of the data inconsistency first makes them sit through context they didn't ask for before getting to what they actually need to know. The explanation itself should translate the technical issue into business terms rather than jargon: instead of 'there's a data quality issue in the source system's order_status field,' something like 'we found that some of the underlying data doesn't match up the way we expected, and using it as-is would give you numbers that look right but are actually wrong -- rather than hand you a metric you can't fully trust, I want to fix the root cause first.' That framing also explains why the delay is worth it, which matters -- a stakeholder who just hears 'it'll be late' with no reason tends to be far less understanding than one who hears 'it'll be late because the alternative is giving you a number that's quietly incorrect.' Offering a concrete new date (Wednesday, not 'soon' or 'a few more days') and, if genuinely useful, a smaller interim option (a rougher version available by Friday with a caveat about what's not yet resolved) respects their need to plan around the delay rather than leaving them with just bad news and no path forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with the headline, not the technical story: 'I want to flag that this is going to take until next Wednesday instead of Friday, and here's why.' Then I'd explain the actual reason in plain terms -- 'while building this, I found that some of the underlying order data doesn't line up the way it should, and if I shipped the dashboard as-is this Friday, the number would look fine but could actually be wrong. I'd rather take the extra few days to fix that at the source than hand you a metric that looks right but isn't.' I think that reasoning matters a lot -- a stakeholder who just hears 'it's delayed' with no explanation is going to be a lot more frustrated than one who hears 'it's delayed because the alternative is handing you a number you can't actually trust.' If there's a genuinely useful partial version I could give them by Friday with a clear caveat on what's not resolved yet, I'd offer that too, so they're not just waiting empty-handed, but I wouldn't pretend a rough number is the real deliverable.
commonMistakes: Leading with technical details of the data issue instead of the practical impact and new timeline
Using jargon ('a data quality issue in the source field') instead of translating the problem into business terms
Giving a vague new timeframe ('soon', 'a bit longer') instead of a concrete new date
Not explaining why the delay is worth it, leaving the stakeholder with just bad news and no context for why it matters
keyPoints: Lead with the practical impact and concrete new timeline, not the technical backstory
Translate the technical issue into business-relevant language, not jargon
Explain why the delay matters -- shipping a wrong number quietly is worse than a short delay
Offer a concrete new date, and a caveated interim option if genuinely useful

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with impact/timeline rather than technical detail
Translates the technical issue into plain, business-relevant language
