Provides a concrete timeline and reasoning for the delay

questions.title: Disagreeing with a teammate's small technical choice
questions.prompt: A teammate on your data engineering team wants to adopt a naming convention for new dbt models that's different from what the rest of the project already uses consistently. You think staying consistent with the existing convention is the better call. How do you raise that disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A disagreement over something like a naming convention is worth raising directly but without treating it as a battle to win -- the useful framing leads with the shared goal (consistency across the project is valuable in itself, independent of which specific convention is 'better' in isolation) rather than with a claim that the teammate's preferred convention is objectively wrong. Something like 'I think I'd lean toward keeping the existing naming pattern just for consistency across the project, even though I can see the appeal of what you're suggesting -- what's driving the change for you?' opens an actual conversation rather than shutting one down, and it genuinely leaves room for the possibility that the teammate has a good reason the existing convention doesn't accommodate well, which is worth hearing before concluding the disagreement is purely stylistic. If after that conversation there's still a genuine disagreement and it's not something either person can simply let go of, the professionally mature move is escalating to whoever has the authority to make a call (a team lead, or raising it as a quick team discussion) rather than letting it quietly fester as an unresolved tension or, worse, having each person build toward their own preferred convention independently and fragmenting the codebase.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd raise it directly, but I'd frame it around the shared value of consistency rather than around 'your idea is wrong.' Something like: 'I think I'd lean toward sticking with our existing naming pattern mainly for consistency across the project -- what's prompting the change for you?' That last part matters to me, because maybe they've hit a real limitation with the current convention that I haven't run into, and I'd rather actually hear that out than assume I already know the full picture. If it turns out this is genuinely just a stylistic preference on both our parts and we still don't agree after talking it through, I wouldn't just let it sit unresolved or have us quietly build toward two different conventions in the same project -- I'd bring it to whoever's the natural tie-breaker, a team lead or just a quick five-minute team discussion, and go with whatever gets decided. The thing I'd specifically avoid is either caving immediately just to avoid friction, or digging in just because I raised it first -- neither of those is actually about getting the right answer for the project.
commonMistakes: Framing the disagreement as 'your idea is wrong' instead of grounding it in the shared value of project-wide consistency
Not asking what's actually motivating the teammate's suggestion before assuming it's purely a stylistic preference
Letting the disagreement go unresolved, risking the codebase fragmenting into two conventions used inconsistently
Either caving immediately to avoid friction or digging in out of ego, instead of focusing on what's actually best for the project
keyPoints: Frame the disagreement around a shared goal (consistency) rather than declaring the other person's idea wrong
Ask what's motivating the suggestion before assuming it's purely stylistic
If unresolved after discussion, escalate to a tie-breaker rather than letting it fester or fragment the codebase
Avoid both reflexively caving and stubbornly digging in -- focus on what's actually best for the project

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames the disagreement constructively around a shared goal
Shows genuine openness to the teammate's reasoning before concluding
Describes a sensible path to resolution if disagreement persists
